documents.title: Knot Tying and Rope Management (TC 3-97.61 Ch. 8)

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management
sections.body:
**Chapter 8**

The rope is a vital piece of equipment to the mountaineer. It is used to address many of the problems and hazards encountered in the mountains. When climbing, rappelling, or building rope installations, the mountaineer must know how to utilize and maintain this equipment.

Misuse can cause serious injury or death. This chapter discusses equipment, terminology, knots, hitches, rope management techniques, care, and maintenance.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: SECTION I – TYPES OF ROPE, WEBBING, AND CARABINERS
sections.body:
8-1. Mountaineering equipment is engineered to be lightweight but strong enough to provide a wide margin of safety. Each item is tested to high standards. In most cases, user error is to blame when this equipment fails. Soldiers should regularly check and inspect mountaineering equipment. Equipment should be replaced when there is any obvious damage, or it has exceeded the manufacturer’s lifecycle recommendation.

8-2. All mountaineering equipment used in training should be constructed and tested to a recognized standard. The International Climbing and Mountaineering Federation, or Union des International Alpine Association (UIAA), is the certifying body that defines the standards for mountaineering and climbing equipment. This safety commission develops the standards for mountaineering and climbing equipment recognized throughout the world. In Europe, the European Conformity, or Conformité Européene (CE), and the European Committee for Standardization establish standards across all industries. They publish standards that align with the UIAA standards for all climbing and mountaineering equipment produced in Europe. The United States has no specific standards, but American manufacturers have their equipment tested to receive UIAA certification. Any equipment used for mountaineering should be marked with either the UIAA safety label or the CE standard that it meets.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: ROPES AND CORDS
Knot Tying and Rope Management: STATIC ROPE
sections.body:
8-5. A static rope is a kernmantle rope designed for minimal stretch under load, primarily used for hauling, lowering, and anchor systems construction. It has a core (kern) that is laid straight, giving it low stretch (2 to 8 percent). They are constructed with a tightly woven sheath (mantle) and are more durable than dynamic ropes. Static ropes are preferred for rappelling, rescue operations, load hauling, and rope installations. They should never be used in situations where the rope is shock loaded (for example, lead climbing). Typical diameter for static rope is between 9 and 11 millimeters (mm). Static rope is issued in 600 feet (183 meters) spools. While the minimum tensile strength for static ropes for military use is 4,500 pounds, the recommended working load is often 25 percent of the actual strength of that rope. The tensile strength for the 9.5 mm-issued low-stretch kernmantle rope is approximately 6,000 pounds. The length needed is dependent on the specific task being conducted. A 45-meter (150 feet) static has been the standard military length since the introduction of nylon ropes, but some tasks or obstacles may require a longer rope. The length of rope over 100 meters is a challenge to carry and manage.

8-6. The military purchases black static ropes to prevent a static rope from being mistaken for a climbing rope; however, static ropes are manufactured in all colors and patterns. A rope of unknown history or construction should not be used for any application.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: DYNAMIC ROPE (CLIMBING ROPE)
sections.body:
8-7. A dynamic rope is a kernmantle rope designed to stretch and absorb force, primarily used to protect climbers from fall injuries. All climbing should be protected with dynamic ropes. Even short falls on static rope can cause serious injury. Standards for climbing ropes are established by the UIAA, and all climbing ropes should be certified.

8-8. Dynamic ropes come in various diameters, but for most military applications, 9 to 10 mm provide a good compromise of durability and weight. The climbing ropes issued in the assault climbing team kits (ACTKs) are 60-meters long but can be cut shorter to meet mission or training requirements. Military climbing ropes are usually produced with olive drab or tan sheaths.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: CORD
sections.body:
8-9. Cord is thinner in diameter than rope. All cord is static and constructed in the same kernmantle structure as larger rope. It is used for constructing anchors, as well as most components in technical rope systems.

Military mountaineering applications work best when Soldiers use 6- to 7-mm diameter cord. It is issued to units on a 200-meter spool and then cut down. It is commonly used in two configurations. Most mountaineering tasks can be accomplished with these two lengths. Units that conduct operations that require ascending a rope or extensive glacier travel may cut additional cords to length for specific tasks:

Cordelette—6-meters long, any appropriate joining knot for anchor construction and general use.

Prusik cord—1.8-meters long, joined with a double fisherman’s bend, for friction hitches.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: WEBBING AND SLINGS
sections.body:
8-10. Webbing is a flat or tubular nylon material that ranges in widths from 9 to 25 mm and has many uses in mountaineering. (See figure 8-2.) This material comes on a spool; it can be cut to a desired length for various purposes. It can be joined or presewn to form slings.

8-11. Slings are presewn or tied loops of webbing. (See figure 8-3, page 152.) A sling is often attached to a harness to act as a personal safety, to extend a rappel device, or attach to a fixed rope. A sling rigged with two carabiners is a runner. Lead climbers use runners to clip the climbing rope to pieces of protection. Most sewn slings are 60 cm and are usually made of nylon.

Sewn slings are made in several lengths: 30 cm, 60 cm, 120 cm, and 180 cm.

Sewn slings are also manufactured with high-strength, low-stretch materials. These are lighter than nylon, do not absorb water, and are more resistant against UV deterioration. However, they are very

static, exhibit very low-melting points, and are not recommended for use as personal safeties or friction hitches.

8-12. If sewn slings are unavailable, tubular webbing can be used to create tied slings. Tubular webbing can be cut to length 175 cm (69 inches) and joined with a water knot to create a sling that is 60 cm (24 inches).

Tied slings can be used for any task as sewn slings but require additional inspection. Tied slings can also be untied and retied around anchors and are more adjustable than sewn slings. Tubular webbing can also be used to create expedient harnesses.

{{img:0}}

{{img:1}}

images.caption: Figure 8-2. Types of webbing: tubular joined with a knot and a sewn webbing

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: CARABINERS
sections.body:
8-13. A carabiner is a D-shaped or oval-shaped metal link, with one spring-hinged side, that is used in mountaineering as a connector between soft materials and to capture a freely running rope. A carabiner is one of the most versatile pieces of equipment available to the mountaineer. This simple piece of gear is the critical connection between anchors, ropes, and mountaineers. (See figure 8-4.)

8-14. Most carabiners are constructed of aluminum. Carabiners are produced in several different shapes. Oval carabiners were once popular for general mountaineering because their symmetry makes them good for many purposes. Most carabiners used today are offset D-shaped carabiners, which offer the best compromise of weight to strength and ease of clipping and racking. (See figure 8-4.)

{{img:0}}

8-15. A carabiner’s design allows it to be loaded in opposite directions along the spine. (See figure 8-4.) When loaded improperly, the strength of a carabiner is reduced significantly. When using a carabiner, care should be taken to avoid cross loading the carabiner across the gate and spine and to avoid tri-loading. (See figure 8-5, page 154.)

8-16. There are two types of carabiners used in mountaineering: the locking carabiner and the nonlocking carabiner.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: LOCKING CARABINERS
sections.body:
8-17. Locking carabiners feature a barrel-shaped sleeve that prevents the gate from opening. They are used where an accidental carabiner opening could cause system failure. Any live load should be attached to an anchor with a locking carabiner. Locking carabiners are used for rappel hook ups, personal safeties, and the primary attachments in most rope systems. (See figure 8-5, page 154.)

{{img:0}}

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: NONLOCKING CARABINERS
sections.body:
8-18. Most carabiners do not lock. Locking mechanisms add weight and slow the manipulation of carabiners.

Nonlocking carabiners are used in most mountaineering applications. They should be used where there is more than one attachment and accidental gate opening will not cause system failure.

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: SECTION II – BASIC TERMINOLOGY**

8-19. Understanding basic terminology is important when learning how to tie knots. The terms explained in this section are the most common in military mountaineering. (See figure 8-6, page 156.)

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: RUNNING END**

8-20. A running end is the loose or working end of the rope.

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: STANDING END**

8-21. The standing end is the static, stationary, or nonworking end of the rope.

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: BIGHT**

8-22. A bight of rope is a bend in the rope in which the standing end is parallel to the running end and the rope does not cross itself.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: LOOP
sections.body:
8-23. A loop is a bend of the rope in which the rope crosses itself. When the running end crosses over the top of the standing end, it is an overhand loop. When the running end crosses under the standing end, it is an underhand loop.

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: TURN**

8-24. A turn wraps around an object, providing 360° contact.

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: ROUND TURN**

8-25. A round turn wraps around an object one and one-half times so that the running and standing end are parallel. A round turn is used to hold an anchor or knot in place.

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: HALF HITCH**

8-26. A half hitch is a turn with the running end crossing over the standing end.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: TAIL
sections.body:
8-27. The tail is the excess portion of the running end of the rope when the knot is completed. If a knot requires an overhand safety, the length of the tail is measured from the safety knot to the end of the rope. A safety knot is a backup knot tied to prevent a primary knot from slipping loose.

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: DRESSING**

8-28. Dressing a knot is arranging all the knot parts, removing unnecessary kinks, twists, and slack so that all rope parts of the knot are secured and tight.

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: SETTING**

8-29. Setting a knot is removing all unnecessary slack from the knot. This ensures that the knot is tight and minimizes the chances of the knot becoming untied.

{{img:0}}

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: SECTION III – KNOT TYING AND CONSIDERATIONS
sections.body:
8-30. The term knot is commonly used to describe numerous categories. A knot is the fixed portion of a rope that has been manipulated around itself, another object, or both during the process of being tied for some purpose. Sometimes it is referred to as a “hard knot” since its condition will remain intact until actively untied. Knots are self-contained and self-supporting and do not need another object or rope to maintain its integrity. Hitches are not considered knots. Yet, for simplicity, they are generalized into a single category.

Knots should never be considered permanent. It is possible that they can loosen or become less secure under certain conditions. Knots should be inspected regularly. Many knots can accomplish the same task; therefore, it is important to understand these considerations when choosing the appropriate knot to tie.

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: TYPES OF KNOTS**

8-31. There are several broad types of knots that are used in mountaineering. Military mountaineers should be familiar with the following types and terms at a minimum.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: BENDS
sections.body:
8-32. Bends are used to join the ends of rope, cord, or webbing. When tied correctly, they are considered safe and strong enough for many applications. Specific joining knots should be used for certain situations and applications. Take care to learn the purpose of each joining knot and to have a clear understanding of where, when, and why to use each one.

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: HITCHES**

8-33. Hitches are like knots but are tied around another object or rope. Without an object like a carabiner or another rope, a hitch would not retain its form and fall apart.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: FRICTION HITCHES
sections.body:
8-34. A friction hitch is a type of hitch tied with webbing or cordage around a rope that can be moved easily while no force is applied to it but cinches and becomes fixed when tensioned. Friction hitches grip the rope while under load, but they can be moved along the rope when unloaded. There are several friction hitches, each with different applications. Using the wrong friction hitch can be dangerous or create additional problems.

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: LOOP KNOTS**

8-35. Loop knots are used to create fixed or adjustable loops in rope or webbing. Some loops are directional to prevent the distortion of a knot when loaded.

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: SPECIALTY KNOTS**

8-36. These knots do not fit the above criteria but are still useful to know. They may only serve one specific purpose for mountaineering.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: KNOT TYING CONSIDERATIONS
sections.body: 8-37. There are several factors to consider when selecting knots for use or training. Military mountaineers do not need to be able to tie every possible knot that can be used in mountaineering. They just need to be able to tie an appropriate knot for each application they may face in their duties. When selecting knots for use in mountaineering rigging, selecting simpler knots that are easier to tie, untie, and inspect are preferable to complex specialty knots, even if the complex knot is a little more effective. When considering teaching knot tying techniques to Soldiers and new military mountaineers, knots that are easier to teach and learn are preferred, as are multipurpose knots. Ultimately, the number and complexity of knots that military mountaineers may need to be proficient with increases as the scope and complexity of their technical mountaineering responsibilities and duties increase.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: STRENGTH

images.caption: Table 8-1. Knotted kernmantle rope retained strength (single strand)

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: EASE OF INSPECTION
sections.body: 8-40. Efficiently inspecting knots is important to ensure they have been tied properly and safely. Choosing knots that are difficult to inspect or that can easily be tied incorrectly heightens the chance of human error and increases risk.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: CONSERVATION OF MATERIAL
sections.body: 8-41. Using as little material as possible is the desired end state in knot tying. Some knots use more material than others do even if they accomplish the same purpose. It is important to recognize this when choosing the appropriate knot for a given application.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: KNOT TYING TECHNIQUES
sections.body:
8-42. More knots exist that are useful to military mountaineering. It is not feasible to include them all in this training circular. Those presented below were selected to cover the full range of military mountaineering applications as simply as possible. Versatility, ease of tying, untying, and teaching were the primary factors considered for selection.

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: OVERHAND SAFETY KNOT**

8-43. An overhand safety is commonly used in conjunction with other knots to make them more secure. Some knots loosen when subject to varying tension and therefore need a backup. (See figure 8-7.)

{{img:0}}

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: INLINE FIGURE EIGHT**

8-44. The inline figure eight is a common initial step in tying figure-eight family knots. (See figure 8-7.)

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: FIGURE-EIGHT SLIP KNOT**

8-45. The figure-eight slip knot forms an adjustable bight in a rope. (See figure 8-8.)

{{img:1}}

images.caption: Figure 8-7. Overhand and inline figure eight

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Checkpoints
sections.body:
8-47. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:

The knot is in the shape of a figure eight.

Both ropes of the bight pass through the same loop of the figure eight.

The sliding portion of the rope is the long working end of the rope.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: FIGURE EIGHT ON A BIGHT (FIGURE-EIGHT LOOP)
sections.body:
8-48. The figure eight on a bight is used to form a fixed loop in a rope. (See figure 8-9.) In certain situations or systems, this knot can be tied with two bights to form two fixed loops (double figure eight on a bight).

This is achieved by folding the cord or rope to form two bights and prior to tying the figure eight.

{{img:0}}

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: Checkpoints**

8-50. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:

The loop is the desired size.

The ropes in the loop are parallel and do not cross over each other.

The knot is tightly dressed.

images.caption: Figure 8-9. Figure eight on a bight

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: FIGURE-EIGHT RETRACE (REROUTED FIGURE EIGHT)
sections.body: 8-51. The rerouted figure-eight knot produces the same result as a figure-eight loop. However, by tying the knot in a retrace, it can be used to tie into a harness or fasten the rope to objects. (See figure 8-10.) It is also called a figure-eight retrace. This is the preferred method to tie into a climbing rope.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Tying the Knot
sections.body:
8-52. The following steps are used to tie a figure-eight retrace:

STEP 1. Tie an inline figure-eight knot, leaving a long enough running end to go around the object or through the harness, and then back through the knot. Leave this knot loose to allow the rope to be routed back through itself easily.

STEP 2. Take the running end and place it through the attachment point on a harness or around an anchor.

STEP 3. With the running end, insert the rope back through the loop of the knot in reverse.

STEP 4. Retrace the knot around the wrap and back to the standing part.

STEP 5. Remove all unnecessary twists and crossovers; dress the knot down.

{{img:0}}

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: Checkpoints**

8-53. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:

- A doubled rope runs side by side in the shape of a figure eight.

The knot forms a fixed loop around a fixed object or harness.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: TWO-LOOP FIGURE EIGHT
sections.body: 8-54. The two-loop figure eight is used to form two adjustable, fixed loops in a rope. (See figure 8-11, page 162.) This knot is useful because it forms two independent loops that are easily adjustable to different lengths.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Tying the Knot
sections.body:
8-55. The following steps are used to tie a two-loop figure eight:

STEP 1. Using a doubled rope, form an 18-inch bight in the left hand with the running end facing the left.

STEP 2. Grasp the bight with the right hand and make a 360° turn around the standing end in a counterclockwise direction.

STEP 3. With the working end, form another bight, then place that bight through the loop just formed in the left hand.

STEP 4. Hold the bight with the left hand, and then place the original bight (moving toward the left hand) over the knot.

STEP 5. Dress the knot down.

{{img:0}}

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Checkpoints
sections.body:
8-56. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:

There is a double figure-eight knot with two loops that share a common locking bar.

The two loops must be adjustable by means of a common locking bar.

The common locking bar is on the bottom of the double figure-eight knot.

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: DIRECTIONAL FIGURE EIGHT**

8-57. The directional figure-eight knot forms a single, fixed loop in the middle of the rope that lays back along the standing part of the rope. (See figure 8-12.)

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Tying the Knot
sections.body:
8-58. The following steps are used to tie a directional figure eight:

STEP 1. Create an overhand loop, with the loop facing the opposite direction of the finished knot.

STEP 2. With the overhand loop formed, tie a figure-eight knot around the standing part.

STEP 3. When dressing the knot down, the running end and the bight must be together.

{{img:0}}

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Checkpoints
sections.body:
8-59. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:

The loop should be large enough to accept a carabiner but no larger than a helmet-size loop.

The tail and bight must be together.

The figure eight is tied tightly.

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: ALPINE BUTTERFLY**

8-60. The alpine butterfly knot forms a single, fixed loop in the middle of the rope. (See figure 8-13, page 164.) The knot can be loaded in either direction or is easy to untie after use.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Tying the Knot
sections.body:
8-61. The following steps are used to tie an alpine butterfly knot:

STEP 1. Take a bight of rope and twist it 360°.

STEP 2. Using the end of the bight, bring it up and back toward the two standing ends that exit at the back of the twisted bight just created. Careful to avoid untwisting the bight while doing this.

STEP 3. Bring the bight back through the portion of the twisted bight that created a hole where the first twist in the bight is located. Pull the bight through that hole.

STEP 4. Next dress down and tighten the knot.

{{img:0}}

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: Checkpoints**

8-62. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:

The knot should have a bight of rope exiting two opposing bights of rope.

The opposing bights should be clean and untwisted.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: FIGURE-EIGHT BEND
sections.body: 8-63. The figure-eight bend is used to join the ends of two ropes of equal or unequal diameter up to a 5-mm difference. (See figure 8-14.) This joining knot should be the primary knot used to join cord. It can be untied after loading, which allows the material to be used for other applications.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Tying the Knot
sections.body:
8-64. The following steps are used to tie a figure-eight bend:

STEP 1. Form a bight in the running end of the rope.

STEP 2. With the other hand, grasp the running end (short end) and make a 360° turn around the standing end.

STEP 3. Place the running end through the loop just formed creating an inline figure eight.

STEP 4. Route the running end of the other rope back through the figure eight starting from the original rope’s running end. Trace the original knot to the standing end.

STEP 5. Remove all unnecessary twists and crossovers. Dress the knot down.

{{img:0}}

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Checkpoints
sections.body:
8-65. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:

There is a figure eight with two ropes running side by side.

The running ends are on opposite sides of the knot.

There is an approximate 4-inch tail.

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: WATER KNOT**

8-66. The water knot is used to attach the ends of webbing. (See figure 8-15.) The water knot is also known as a ring bend or tape knot.

{{img:0}}

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Checkpoints
sections.body:
8-68. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:

There are two overhand knots, one retracing the other.

There is no slack in the knot, and the working ends come out of the knot in opposite directions.

There is an approximate 4-inch tail.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: FLAT OVERHAND
sections.body:
8-69. The flat overhand is used for joining two ropes that are being used to rappel. (See figure 8-16.) Additionally, it is used as a stopper knot at the end of the ropes to prevent Soldiers from rappelling off the end of the ropes.

{{img:0}}

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: Checkpoints**

8-71. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:

- A double overhand dressed without twists.

- Minimum 18-inch tails.

- Knot should be hard to the touch, not loose, or sloppy.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: DOUBLE FISHERMAN’S KNOT
sections.body: 8-72. The double fisherman’s knot is used to join the ends of a rope of the same diameter. (See figure 8-17.) Once loaded, it can become very difficult to untie. Avoid using this knot if it must be untied after use.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Tying the Knot
sections.body:
8-73. The following steps are used to tie a double fisherman’s knot:

{{img:0}}

STEP 1. With the working end of one rope, tie two wraps around the standing part of another rope.

STEP 2. Insert the working end (step 1) back through the two wraps and draw it tight.

STEP 3. With the working end of the other rope, which contains the standing part (steps 1 and 2), tie two wraps around the standing part of the other rope, routing the wraps in the opposite direction as the first knot (the working end in step 1). Insert the working end back through the two wraps and draw tight.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Checkpoints
sections.body:
8-74. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:

Two double overhand knots securing each other as the standing parts of the rope are pulled apart.

Four rope parts on one side of the knot form two X patterns; four rope parts on the other side of the knot are parallel.

Ends of rope exit knot opposite each other with approximately 4-inch tails.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: SQUARE KNOT
sections.body: 8-75. The square knot is used to join the ends of rope of equal diameter while under tension. (See figure 8-18, page 170.) This joining knot should only be used when it is impossible to tie a more secure joining knot like the figure-eight bend or double fisherman’s knot.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Tying the Knot
sections.body:
8-76. The following steps are used to tie a square knot:

STEP 1: Holding one working end in each hand, place the working end in the right hand over the one in the left hand.

STEP 2: Pull it under and back over the top of the rope in the left hand.

STEP 3: Place the working end in the left hand over the one in the right hand and repeat step 2.

STEP 4: Dress the knot down and secure it with an overhand knot on each side of the square knot.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Checkpoints
sections.body:
{{img:0}}

8-77. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:

There are two interlocking bights.

The running end and standing part are on the same side of the bight formed by the other rope.

The running ends are parallel to and on the same side of the standing ends with 4-inch minimum tails after the overhand safeties are tied.

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: BOWLINE**

8-78. The bowline is used to tie the end of a rope around an anchor. It may also be used to tie a single fixed loop at the end of a rope. (See figure 8-19.)

{{img:1}}

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Checkpoints
sections.body:
8-80. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:

The bight is locked into place by a loop.

The short portion of the bight is on the inside and on the loop around the anchor (or inside the fixed loop).

There is an approximate 4-inch tail after tying the overhand safety.

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: TRIPLE BOWLINE (THREE-LOOP BOWLINE)**

8-81. The triple bowline is used to tie the middle or a bight of rope around an anchor. (See figure 8-20.)

{{img:0}}

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Checkpoints
sections.body:
8-83. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:

There are two bights held in place by two loops.

The bights form locking bars around the standing end.

There is an approximate 4-inch tail (bight) after the double overhand safety knot is tied.

The running end (bight) must be on the inside of the fixed loops.

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: BOWLINE ON A BIGHT (TWO-LOOP BOWLINE)**

8-84. The bowline on a bight is used to form two fixed loops in the middle of a rope. (See figure 8-21.)

{{img:0}}

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: Checkpoints**

8-86. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:

There are two fixed loops that will not slip.

There are no twists in the knot.

- A double loop is held in place by a bight.

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: GIRTH HITCH**

8-87. The girth hitch is used to attach a cord or sling to an anchor or piece of equipment. (See figure 8-22.) The hitch is also used to attach a sling to a harness.

{{img:1}}

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: Checkpoints**

8-89. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:

Two wraps exist with a locking bar running across the wraps.

The knot is dressed tightly.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: PRUSIK
sections.body: 8-90. The prusik is a friction hitch that can be loaded in either direction. When force is applied to this friction hitch, it is very difficult to move or loosen. It can be tied with the middle or end of a cord.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Tying the Knot
sections.body:
8-91. The prusik can be tied with a cordelette to an installation rope. An installation rope is the primary load-bearing rope or strand in a rope system. A minimum of three turns should be used for this knot. The closer in diameter the cordelette is to the installation rope, the more turns may be required for the knot to function. Ideally, there should be a 3-mm difference in diameter between the cordelette and installation rope.

Always check to see if the prusik grabs prior to operation.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Middle-of-the-Rope Prusik
sections.body:
8-92. The following steps are used to tie a middle-of-the-rope prusik (see figure 8-23):

STEP 1. Double the cord, forming a bright, with the working ends even. Lay it over the installation rope so that the closed end of the bight is below the installation rope and the remaining part of the rope (working ends) is the closest. Spread the working end apart.

STEP 2. Reach down through the 12-inch bight. Pull up both working ends and lay them over the installation rope. Repeat this process twice more, making sure that the working ends pass in the

middle of the first two turns. Now there are six turns and a locking bar working across them on the installation rope.

{{img:0}}

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: End-of-the-Rope Prusik
sections.body:
8-93. The following steps are used to tie an end-of-the-rope prusik (see figure 8-24, page 176):

STEP 1. Take approximately 1 meter of cord and place it over the installation rope.

STEP 2. Form a complete round turn in the rope.

STEP 3. Cross over the standing part of the cord with the working end of the cord.

STEP 4. Lay the working end under the installation rope.

STEP 5. Form a complete round turn in the rope, working back toward the middle of the knot.

STEP 6. There are six turns and a locking bar running across them on the installation rope. Dress the wraps and locking bar down. Ensure they are tight, parallel, and untwisted.

STEP 7. Finish the knot with a bowline with the tail, ensure both strands have tension on it and running end of the prusik knot cannot be pulled through and undo the knot.

{{img:0}}

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Checkpoints
sections.body:
8-94. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:

Six complete turns with a locking bar.

The knot is tight and dressed down with no ropes twisted or crossed.

The end-of-the-rope prusik hitch should be closed out with a bowline to prevent slipping.

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: AUTOBLOCK**

8-95. The autoblock creates a friction hitch that is releasable even when force is applied. (See figure 8-25.) This knot is used as a hands-free backup for rappelling and lowering.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Tying the Knot
sections.body:
8-96. The following steps are used to tie an autoblock knot:

STEP 1. Begin with a joined length of webbing or cord about 24-inches long. A presewn sling is also acceptable.

STEP 2. Offset the joining knot, keeping it close to one end of the loop. If using sewn webbing, treat the sewn portion as the knot.

STEP 3. Begin wrapping the clean portion of material around the rope. Create a minimum of three complete turns.

STEP 4. Secure both bights into a locking carabiner that is attached to the harness and lock it.

STEP 5. Ensure the autoblock grabs the rope by testing it prior to use. Smaller diameter ropes may require more than four wraps.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Checkpoints
sections.body:
{{img:0}}

8-97. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:

Both bights of the joined material are secured into a locking carabiner.

There is a minimum of three turns.

The joining knot, tails, or sewn portion is not incorporated into any of the wraps or in the carabiner.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: KLEMHEIST
sections.body:
8-98. The klemheist is a friction hitch. Like the prusik, it is difficult to move or loosen while force is being applied. It is easier and quicker to tie than the prusik. It is also easier to loosen and move after applying force than the prusik. It cannot be loaded in both directions. (See figure 8-26, page 178.)

{{img:0}}

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: Checkpoints**

8-100. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:

The bight is opposite the direction of pull.

- All wraps are tight and touching.

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: BACHMANN HITCH**

8-101. The Bachmann hitch is a friction hitch that is easily released and reset. (See figure 8-27.) The carabiner acts as a handle to help move the friction hitch along the rope.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Tying the Knot
sections.body:
8-102. The following steps are used to tie a Bachmann hitch:

STEP 1. Find the middle of a cordelette and insert it into a carabiner.

STEP 2. Place the carabiner and cordelette next to the installation rope.

STEP 3. With the two ropes parallel from the carabiner, make two or more wraps around the climbing rope and through the inside portion of the carabiner.

{{img:0}}

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Checkpoints
sections.body:
8-103. The following must be true for a knot to be correct:

The bight of the climbing rope is at the top of the carabiner.

The two ropes run parallel without twisting or crossing.

Two or more wraps are made around the long climbing rope and through the inside portion of the carabiner.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: CLOVE HITCH
sections.body:
8-104. The clove hitch is an anchor knot that can be used in the middle of the rope as well as at the end. (See figure 8-28, page 180 and figure 8-29, page 181.) This hitch is easily adjustable after it has been tied and it uses a little rope.

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: Tying the Knot**

8-105. There are two versions of the clove hitch: the middle-of-the-rope clove hitch and the end-of-the-rope clove hitch.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Middle-of-the-Rope Clove Hitch
sections.body:
8-106. The following steps are used to tie a middle-of-the-rope clove hitch (see figure 8-28, page 180):

STEP 1. Hold the rope in both hands, palms down with hands together. Slide the left hand to the left approximately 10 inches.

STEP 2. Form a loop away from and back toward the right.

STEP 3. Slide the right hand approximately 10 inches to the right. Form a loop inward and back to the left hand.

STEP 4. Place the left loop on top of the right loop. Place both loops over the anchor and pull both ends of the rope in opposite directions.

{{img:0}}

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: End-of-the-Rope Clove Hitch
sections.body:
8-107. The following steps are used to tie an end-of-the-rope clove hitch (see figure 8-29):

STEP 1. Place approximately 30 inches of rope over the top of the anchor. Hold the standing end in the left hand. With the right hand, reach under the horizontal anchor, grasp the working end, and bring it inward.

STEP 2. Place the working end of the rope over the standing end (to form a loop). Hold the loop in the left hand. Place the working end over the anchor to the left of the loop.

STEP 3. With the right hand, reach down to the left-hand side of the loop under the anchor. Grasp the working end of the rope. Bring the working end up and outward.

STEP 4. Dress down the knot.

{{img:0}}

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Checkpoints
sections.body:
8-108. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:

The knot has two round turns around the anchor with a diagonal locking bar.

The locking bar is facing 90° from the direction of pull.

The ends exit l80° from each other.

The knot has more than a 4-inch tail remaining.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: MUNTER HITCH
sections.body: 8-109. The Munter hitch is used to form a mechanical belay. (See figure 8-30, page 182.) The Munter hitch produces friction, reducing the force required to hold a fall. It can be used to belay a climber going up or to lower a climber or load down.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Tying the Knot
sections.body:
8-110. The following steps are used to tie a Munter hitch:

STEP 1. Hold the rope in both hands, palms down about 12 inches apart.

STEP 2. With the right hand, form a loop away from the body toward the left hand. Hold the loop with the left hand.

STEP 3. With the right hand, place the rope that comes from the bottom of the loop over the top of the loop.

STEP 4. Place the bight that has just been formed around the rope into a locking carabiner. Secure the locking carabiner.

The carabiner is locked.

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: Checkpoints**

8-111. The following must be true for the knot to be correct: A bight passes through the carabiner with the close end around the standing or running part of the rope.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: SUPER MUNTER HITCH
sections.body:
{{img:0}}

8-112. The super Munter hitch is used to form a high-friction lower. (See figure 8-31.) The knot produces more friction with an additional wrap. Mountaineers use the super Munter hitch to lower very heavy loads.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Tying the Knot
sections.body:
8-113. The following steps are used to tie a super Munter hitch:

STEP 1. Hold the rope in both hands, palms down about 12 inches apart.

STEP 2. With the right hand, form a loop away from the body toward the left hand. Hold the loop with the left hand.

STEP 3. With the right hand, place the rope that comes from the bottom of the loop over the top of the loop.

STEP 4. Place the bight that has just been formed around the rope into a locking carabiner.

STEP 5. Take the brake strand or the strand not exiting the carabiner into the bight and pass it under the knot and carabiner. (A brake strand is the strand of a rope system that controls the rate at which a load is lowered or a rappeller descends.) Then bring it back up to form another bight.

Take this bight and place it into the locking carabiner. Secure the carabiner.

{{img:0}}

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Checkpoints
sections.body:
8-114. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:

- A bight passes through the carabiner, with the closed end around the standing or running part of the

rope.

- An additional opposite bight is wrapped around the same strand as the first.

The carabiner is locked.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: MUNTER MULE KNOT
sections.body:
8-115. The mule knot is used to create an easily releasable anchor knot in conjunction with a Munter hitch. (See figures 8-32 and 8-33, page 184.) This knot is used in systems where there is a need for releasability.

The mule knot can be used to tie off a belay or lower to go hands free.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Tying the Knot
sections.body:
8-116. The following steps are used to tie a Munter mule knot:

STEP 1. Place a Munter hitch into a locking carabiner.

STEP 2. With the brake strand of the Munter, create an overhand loop and place onto the load strand of the Munter hitch.

STEP 3. Bring a bight through the overhand loop, capturing the load strand creating a slipknot.

STEP 4. Dress the slipknot down against the Munter hitch.

STEP 5. Pass the tails through the bight of the slipknot.

STEP 6. Dress the bight to 4 to 6 inches.

{{img:0}}

{{img:1}}

images.caption: Figure 8-32. Munter mule knot using cord
Figure 8-33. Munter mule knot using installation rope

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Checkpoints
sections.body:
8-117. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:

- A bight passes through the carabiner, with the closed end around the standing or running part of the

rope.

- An additional opposite bight is wrapped around the same strand as the first.

The carabiner is locked.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: GARDA HITCH
sections.body:
8-118. The garda hitch (ratchet knot, alpine clutch) is a special-purpose knot, which allows rope to travel in one direction but not the other. The garda hitch is primarily used for hauling systems or rescue. (See figure 8-34.) The knot works in only one direction, and it cannot be reversed while under load.

{{img:0}}

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: Checkpoints**

8-120. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:

- When properly dressed, rope can only be pulled in one direction.

The knot will not fail when placed under load.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: BIG HONKING KNOT
sections.body: 8-121. The big honking knot (BHK) is used to bring together strands of rope from multiple anchors to create a master point. (See figure 8-35, page 186.) It is often used in institutional top rope and rappel anchors. The BHK is a strong, secure knot that can handle repeated use, yet is still easy to untie.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Tying the Knot
sections.body:
8-122. The following steps are used to tie a BHK:

STEP 1. Equalize all the strands from the anchor points, then fold back approximately 24 inches of the bight that is created.

STEP 2. Tie a double overhand or figure-eight knot with all the strands.

STEP 3. Check that all loops are fixed. The loop that exits behind the knot, toward the anchors, should be secured, either with a carabiner to one of the anchor legs or by passing the knot through the loop adding extra security.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Checkpoints
sections.body:
{{img:0}}

8-123. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:

There are two fixed loops that exit away from the anchors.

Four strands of rope should exit together from the back of the knot toward the anchors.

Two of the strands in the back form an additional fixed loop.

This fixed loop should be secured by a carabiner attached to a leg of the anchor or the knot should be passed through this loop to ensure it cannot be pulled back through the knot.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: FIELD EXPEDIENT HARNESS
sections.body: 8-124. The field expedient harness creates a seat harness out of tubular webbing used for climbing or rappelling. (See figure 8-36, page 188.) This improvised harness is more secure than the rappel seat and will not come loose while climbing. The field expedient harness can also be used in rescue to secure a patient not wearing a harness. Either 1- or 2-inch tubular webbing is acceptable for use.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Constructing the Harness
sections.body:
8-125. The following steps are used to tie a field expedient harness:

STEP 1. Find the middle of a 25-foot section of tubular webbing and form a bight.

STEP 2. Pass the bight between the legs from rear to front and pull it up to beltline level.

STEP 3. Wrap the right and left tails of webbing around each respective leg from rear to front ensuring that the tails do not cross over one another.

STEP 4. Pass the tails through the bight at belt level and wrap them back onto themselves.

STEP 5. Wrap the remaining lengths of webbing around the body above the hips and continue to wrap in the opposite directions until enough is remaining to tie a square knot with safeties.

STEP 6. Join the tails together just above the hip offset from front of the body on either side of the body using a square knot with overhand safeties.

{{img:0}}

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Checkpoints
sections.body:
8-126. The following must be true for the knot to be correct:

Tails are passed through the diaper portion to create leg loops in the same direction.

- Webbing does not cross between the legs.

- Minimum one full wrap around the body above the hips.

Secured on one hip with a square knot. Safeties are only tied around the last strand around the waist.

Square knot is far enough to the side that anything tied or clipped into the harness does not hit the square knot.

SECTION IV – ROPES: PREPARATION, CARE, INSPECTION, COILING,

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: CARRYING, AND THROWING
sections.body: 8-127. The service life of a rope depends on the frequency of use, applications (rappelling, climbing, rope installations), speed of descent, surface abrasion, terrain, climate, and quality of maintenance. Ropes may fail if misused, placed over sharp edges, or not properly inspected prior to use.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: PREPARING ROPES
sections.body:
8-128. The mountaineer must select the proper rope for the task to be accomplished according to type, diameter, length, and breaking strength. It is important to prepare all ropes before departing on a mission.

Avoid rope preparation in the field.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: PACKAGING
sections.body:
8-129. New rope comes from the manufacturer in different configurations, boxed on a spool in various lengths, or coiled and bound in some manner. New ropes should be carefully unspooled or uncoiled to avoid kinks and prevent tangling.

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: Coil**

8-130. A coil is a secure configuration of rope that allows for easy transport without tangling.

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: Precut**

8-131. Precut ropes are usually packaged in a protective cover, such as plastic.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: SECURING THE ENDS OF ROPE
sections.body: 8-132. If still on a spool, the rope must be cut to the desired length. All ropes fray at the ends unless they are bound or seared. Both static and dynamic rope ends are secured in the same manner. The ends must be heated to the melting point to attach the inner core strands to the outer sheath. By fusing the two together, the sheath cannot slide backward or forward. Ensure that this is only done to the ends of the rope. If the rope is exposed to extreme temperatures, the sheath could be weakened, along with the inner core, reducing overall tensile strength. The ends may also be dipped in enamel or lacquer for further protection.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: CARE AND MAINTENANCE
sections.body:
8-133. The rope is a climber’s lifeline. The rope must be maintained and used properly. Climbers should use the following general guidelines when handling ropes:

- While in use, do not allow the rope to touch sharp edges. Rope is cut more easily when under tension.

If the rope must be used over a sharp edge, pad the edge for protection and inspect often.

- Never allow one rope to continuously run over another. The friction causes the nylon to melt.

- Never leave a rope knotted or tightly stretched for longer than necessary. Doing so reduces the

strength and life of the rope over time.

- UV radiation (sunlight) tends to deteriorate nylon over long periods. This becomes important if rope

installations are left in place for months.

- Do not step on or drag ropes on the ground unnecessarily. Small particles of dirt grind between the

inner strands slowly cutting them.

- All ropes should be washed periodically to remove dirt and grit and rinsed thoroughly. Army-issued rope washes are made from short pieces of modified pipe that connect to any faucet. Pinholes within the pipe force water to circulate around and scrub the rope as the Soldier slowly feeds it through the washer. Ropes should not be stored wet. Dry wet ropes by uncoiling and hanging them in large loops off the ground. Never dry a rope with high heat or in direct sunlight.

- When not in use, ropes should be loosely coiled and hung on wooden pegs rather than nails or other metal objects. Storage areas should be relatively cool with low-humidity levels to prevent mildew

or rotting. Rope may also be loosely stacked and placed in a rope bag and stored on a shelf. Avoid storage in direct sunlight, as the UV radiation deteriorates the nylon over long periods.

Inspect the rope before each use for frayed or cut spots, mildew or rot, or defects in construction (new rope).

- Do not mark ropes with paints or allow them to touch oils or petroleum products. Some of these

weaken or deteriorate nylon.

- Never subject the rope to high heat or flame. Heat and flame significantly weaken rope.

- Never use a mountaineering rope for any purpose except mountaineering.

Each rope should have a corresponding rope log DA Form 5752-R (Rope Log [Usage and History]), which is also a safety record. On the form, annotate use, terrain, weather, application, number of falls, dates, and so on. Annotate each time the rope is used on the form. DA Form 5752-R is authorized for local reproduction on 8 1/2- by 11-inch paper.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: INSPECTION
sections.body:
8-134. Ropes should be inspected before and after each use, especially when working around loose rock or sharp edges.

- Although the core of the kernmantle rope cannot be seen, it is possible to damage the core without damaging the sheath. Check a kernmantle rope by carefully inspecting the sheath before and after use while the rope is being coiled. When coiling, be aware of how the rope feels as it runs through the hands. Immediately note and tie off any lumps or depressions felt.

- Damage to the core of a kernmantle rope usually consists of filaments or yarn breakage that results in a slight retraction. If enough strands rupture, a localized reduction in the diameter of the rope results in a depression that can be felt or even seen. Check any other suspected areas further by putting them under tension (the weight of one person, approximately 185 pounds standing on a prusik tensioning system is about maximum). This procedure emphasizes the lump or depression by separating the broken strands and enlarging the dip. If a noticeable difference in diameter is obvious, retire the rope immediately.

- Many dynamic kernmantle ropes are quite soft. They may retain an indentation occasionally after an impact or under normal use without any trauma to the core. When damage is suspected, patiently inspect the sheath for abnormalities. Damage to the sheath does not always mean damage to the core. Inspect carefully.

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: COILING AND CARRYING ROPE**

8-135. Use the butterfly or mountain coil to coil and carry the rope. Each is easy to accomplish and results in a minimal number of kinks, twists, and knots later during deployment.

**Knot Tying and Rope Management: BUTTERFLY COIL**

8-136. The butterfly coil is the quickest and easiest technique for coiling. (See figure 8-37.)

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Coiling
sections.body: 8-137. To start the butterfly coil, grasp both ends of the rope and begin back stacking, ensuring the ends of the rope are not buried at the bottom of the stack. Find the center of the rope and form a bight. With the bight in the left hand, grasp both ropes and slide the right hand out until there is approximately one arm-length of rope. Place the doubled rope over the head, draping it around the neck and over the shoulders. Ensure that it hangs no lower than the waist. Soldiers ensure the rest of the doubled rope is in front of them and continue making doubled bights and placing them over the head in the same manner as the first bight. Coil alternating from side to side (left to right, right to left) while maintaining equal-length bights. Continue coiling until approximately two arm-lengths of rope remain. Remove the coils from the neck and shoulders and hold the center in one hand. Wrap the two ends upwards around the coils with a minimum of three complete wraps, ensuring that the first wrap locks back on itself.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: Tie Off and Carrying
sections.body:
8-138. Take both strands from the tails of the rope, forming a double bight and pass it through the apex of the coils. Pull the loose ends through the doubled bight and dress it down. Ensure that the loose ends do not exceed 2 meters. In this configuration, the coiled rope is secure enough for hand carrying or carrying in a rucksack or for storage. To carry on the body, place the butterfly coil on the back, with one tail over each of the shoulders, bring back directly under the arms and wrap at least once around the body, ensuring to capture all the coils. Secure the ends with a square knot, which does not need overhand safeties. (See figure 8-37 for a farmer’s tie off.)

{{img:0}}

images.caption: Figure 8-37. Butterfly coil with farmer’s tie off

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: MOUNTAIN COIL
sections.body:
8-139. To start a mountain coil, grasp the rope about 1 meter from the end with one hand. Run the other hand along the rope until both arms are outstretched. Grasping the rope firmly, bring the hands together, forming a loop, which is laid in the hand closest to the end of the rope. This is repeated, forming uniform loops that run in a clockwise direction, until the rope is completely coiled. The rope may be given a one-quarter twist as each loop is formed to overcome any tendency for the rope to twist or form figure eights.

8-140. To finish the mountain coil, form a bight about 30-cm long with the starting end of the rope and lay it along the top of the coil. Uncoil the last loop and, using this length of the rope, begin making wraps around the coil and the bight, wrapping toward the closed end of the bight. Make six to eight wraps to adequately secure the coil, and then route the end of the rope through the closed end of the bight. Pull the running end of the bight tight, securing the coil.

8-141. The mountain coil may be carried in either the pack (by forming a figure eight), doubling it and placing it under the flap, or by placing it over the shoulder and under the opposite arm, slung across the chest. (Figure 8-38 shows how to coil a mountain coil.)

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: COILING CORDS AND SLINGS
sections.body:
{{img:0}}

8-142. Length of cord, webbing, or rope less than 8 meters may be coiled so that they can be hung from the harness. Hold the ends of the cord or the joining knot in the left hand. Coil the doubled rope into 6- to 8-inch loops until an approximate 12-inch bight is left. Wrap that bight around the coil, ensuring that the first wrap locks on itself. Wrap until there is just enough bight left to feed through the bights formed at the top of the coil. Dress it down tightly. Now the piece of rope or webbing may be hung from a carabiner on the harness or attached to a gear sling and slung over the shoulder. The same can be done with slings.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: UNCOILING, BACK STACKING, AND STACKING
sections.body:
8-143. When the rope is needed for use, it must be uncoiled and back stacked on the ground properly to avoid kinks and snarls. Choose a location that is clear of sharp rocks, sticks, or other items that could damage the rope or cause snarls when deploying the rope. Also, avoid wet or muddy areas. When these locations are unavoidable, using a tarp, poncho, or rope bag to place under the rope when stacking can provide protection.

8-144. Untie the tie off and lay the coil on the ground. Single back stack the rope to minimize kinks and snarls. (This is also useful when moving the rope a short distance and coiling is not desired.) Take one end of the rope in the left hand and run the right hand along the rope until both arms are outstretched. Next, lay the end of the rope in the left hand on the ground, ensuring that the standing end of the rope is laid off to the side and is not buried under the stack. With the left hand, regrasp the rope next to the right hand and continue laying the rope on the ground.

8-145. The rope should be laid or stacked in a neat pile on the ground to prevent it from becoming tangled and knotted when throwing the rope, feeding it to a lead climber, and so on. This technique can also be started using the right hand.

sections.heading: Knot Tying and Rope Management: THROWING THE ROPE
sections.body:
8-146. Before throwing the rope, it should be back stacked to prevent it from tangling during deployment.

The bottom end of the rope should be anchored to prevent complete loss of the rope over the edge when it is thrown. Several techniques can be used when deploying a rope.

8-147. If the cliff is steep enough, it may be unnecessary to throw the rope. Back stack the rope down the cliff face. The rope is less likely to be carried by the wind or to be caught in trees. It is more likely to be hung up on ledges and shrubs on the face than when thrown. The rope should be thrown at a low angle and blocky terrain.

8-148. To throw the rope, take the strand on the top of the stack and begin to create butterfly coils in the dominant hand. Create enough coils so that there is sufficient weight to carry the rest of the rope down when it is thrown. It is time consuming and almost never necessary to coil the entire length of rope to throw it. The rope is best thrown underhand and slightly up and out from the edge. Throwing the rope too high could cause it to be hung up in tree branches. At a training site where there may be people below, the thrower should confirm that no one is below and sound off with the following warning as they throw: ROPE.

8-149. When windy weather conditions prevail, adjustments must be made. In a strong crosswind, the rope should be thrown angled into the wind so that it lands on the desired target. The stronger the wind, the harder the rope must be thrown to compensate. If the wind is too strong, sometimes it is best to single back stack the rope in a pack. The first Soldier who descends the rope should guide it down the fall line. During the descent, the rope is stacked in such a way that it exits cleanly from the pack to avoid becoming tangled.

Another technique is to coil the rope freely on the shoulders of the first Soldier, allowing it to easily uncoil as the Soldier descends.

8-150. This Soldier needs to incorporate a hands-free backup during the rappel to allow stopping and using both hands to manage the rope, if necessary.

documents.title: Crossing Mountain Streams (TC 3-97.61 Ch. 13)

sections.heading: Mountain Stream Crossing
sections.body:
**Chapter 13**

In 480 BC, Persian King Xerxes constructed a pontoon bridge that spanned a mile and a quarter across the Hellespont. After a previous failure to take Greece, the king weighed the options of either finding alternate routes to the north that added months to his expedition or pinpoint potential water crossing locations for his army. Xerxes insisted on the fastest and most direct route across the Aegean inlet for his 300,000 men. While negotiating the linear obstacle involved massive resources and engineering, it would save precious time for his army to reach their objective.

sections.heading: Mountain Stream Crossing: SECTION I – MOUNTAIN STREAM FUNDAMENTALS
sections.body:
13-1. A mountain stream crossing is essentially an approach to negotiating a potentially swift and cold waterway that Soldiers may encounter in the mountains. Learning to cross small streams forms a foundation of skills for personnel to manage larger streams and rivers, where consequences could be far more hazardous.

13-2. In an operation involving the crossing of a stream or river, the actual crossing itself is a means, not an end sought. The purpose is for designated units to conduct a crossing to establish security on the far bank to protect remaining personnel. This operation should be conducted economically and with minimal loss of momentum.

13-3. There are limits on the safe use of the techniques discussed in this chapter. Not all mountain rivers or streams will be fordable with these techniques. If a water obstacle is too wide, swift, or deep, an alternate route should be used. It may require using aircraft transport if engineer support is unavailable.

Reconnaissance of questionable crossing sites is essential. This chapter covers the techniques for crossing mountain streams that have a depth generally not exceeding waist level.

13-4. Stream crossings should not be taken lightly. The force of flowing water may be extremely great and is most often underestimated. All rivers and streams are obstacles to movement. They should be treated as danger areas and avoided whenever possible. When rivers or streams must be crossed, there are many techniques that the small-unit leader may choose from, depending upon the type of stream, its width, speed of the current, and depth of the water. This activity should be rehearsed prior to execution in the operational environment.

sections.heading: Mountain Stream Crossing: RECONNAISSANCE
sections.body:
13-5. Performing a site survey of potential crossing locations (map, photo, or aerial) may not always reveal that a water obstacle exists. In a swamp, for example, unfordable sloughs may not show on the map, and they may be concealed from aerial observation by a canopy of vegetation.

13-6. Site selection is extremely important once Soldiers determine that they must make a crossing. Elevated positions offer an optimal vantage point from which to analyze a large area of possibilities. This is sometimes better than a hundred close views from a riverbank. Select the site selection before the main body arrives and examine the site around a similar time of day that the crossing will be conducted.

13-7. A suitable crossing site should have specific characteristics. A river crossing site should limit exposure to observation, facilitate the installation team crossing (if necessary) or swimming with ropes, and minimize drowning hazards. Care must be taken to avoid an installation team crossing upstream of rapids, waterfalls, or fallen trees in the river. For dry features, such as gorges or ravines, the site should facilitate the installation team’s descent and ascent crossing while minimizing any falling hazards that exist. While dry crossings are preferred to wet crossings for speed and safety factors, they can become locations for an enemy to place landmines and improvised explosive devices.

13-8. The time of day is an important factor. Recent precipitation or increased temperatures could cause water levels to rise as glaciers or snow-covered peaks begin to melt. Early morning crossings are preferred, as the cooler night temperatures usually reduce the melt from snow and ice. A morning crossing also allows clothing items to dry throughout the day. Whether a crossing is made in daylight or in darkness depends on

the need for concealment, proficiency of troops, nature of the terrain, characteristics of the water obstacle, enemy disposition and capabilities (such as minefields on far banks), and the need for speed.

13-9. A crossing point should be chosen where the river widens. The sudden width of the channel normally yields a shallow depth. Avoid sharp turns in the river or a narrowing choke point in the river or stream since the water is likely to be deep and have a strong current on the outside of the bend for curves.

13-10. Many mountain streams, especially those fed by glacier runoff, contain sections with numerous braided channels. While often shallower than a main river, this changing landscape offers little in the way of cover and concealment of exposed personnel. Shoals, or partially submerged sandbars, can act like quicksand depending on the riverbed composition.

13-11. Riverbanks should be low enough to accommodate for easy entry and exit from the water. Banks that are tall and steep may require employing installations such as hasty rappels (see figure 11-11, page 293) or simple fixed ropes (see figure 11-2, page 278).

13-12. Logjams and other large obstructions present their own hazards. Floating debris, while often hung up in shallow spots, can potentially hit personnel in the water. Water flowing around logjams creates riverbed erosion and swift waters. If crossing upstream of logjams, ensure that Soldiers are far enough away to react and do not become entangled in branches beneath the water surface.

13-13. When possible, cross with ample overwatch in place for support and with an approach that offers minimal detection by enemy forces.

sections.heading: Mountain Stream Crossing: PREPARATION OF TROOPS AND EQUIPMENT
sections.body:
13-14. Special considerations should be taken for personnel and the items they carry for the mission. Water can weigh personnel down, as can the uniform posture when dealing with submerged equipment. Most of the preparation should happen long before entering the water, with only special considerations executed in a short halt prior. Preparation should include—

- Water-sensitive items. Wrap radios, binoculars, documents, maps, and any extra clothing in waterproof bags (trash bags also work well), if available. These bags also provide additional flotation, should Soldiers find themselves in deeper water than expected. Pack these dry clothing items on top, along with other necessary items (such as munitions, sensitive items, and machine gun tripods) quickly before getting into the water.

- Uniform. If the tactical situation permits, a crossing can be made with minimal clothing. Once on the far side, Soldiers can change into dry clothing. Normally, a complete uniform is worn. Unblouse boots and untuck shirts. Ensure all pockets are buttoned or closed. If water has a point of entry, ensure that it has an easy way to exit. Trapped water can weigh down personnel who may need to swim at a moment’s notice. Socks and boot insoles can be removed and stowed. Once on the far bank, boots can be drained, and wet socks replaced. Load-carrying equipment and body armor. Unbuckle fighting load carrier or other modular equipment and be prepared to remove, if necessary. It is difficult to remove a buckled harness in the water during an emergency.

- Helmets can be removed and stowed, but if Soldiers fall in water with debris, the helmet protects

their head from impacts.

The rucksack should be worn well up on the shoulders and snug, so it does not flop around and cause imbalance. The waist and chest straps must be unbuckled so Soldiers can rid themselves of the rucksack if they are swept off their feet and must resort to swimming. Securing everything inside the pack will help if it needs to be discarded. It is easier to find one large pack than several smaller items.

- Weapons should be secured to the pack or slung over the shoulder.

sections.heading: Mountain Stream Crossing: SECTION II – CROSSING TECHNIQUES
sections.body:
13-15. Several techniques and methods exist to successfully negotiate water obstacles. Variables that can influence the most optimal crossing style are water depth and speed, confidence around water and swimming

proficiency, riverbed surface, daylight or night crossing, and resources available. When available, a dry crossing is always preferred.

13-16. In this section, we will discuss three different variations that work well for mountain stream crossings: the individual crossing, team crossing, and belayed crossing.

sections.heading: Mountain Stream Crossing: INDIVIDUAL CROSSINGS
sections.body:
13-17. Whenever possible, and when the degree of experience permits, streams should be forded individually for a speedier crossing. (See figure 13-1.) The average Soldier should be able to cross most streams with mild to moderate currents and water depths of not much more than knee-deep using proper techniques. An advantage to the individual crossing is that there is nothing to recover once Soldiers have performed the crossing. A disadvantage is the time of exposure for the individual and time invested for the element to negotiate the water obstacle.

13-18. The water depth at a suitable crossing site should be about knee height or below, and the water’s speed should be mild to moderate. The velocity of the water and the presence of debris are used to determine the effect, if any, on the ford’s condition. Currents are categorized as—ν Swift (more than 1.5 meters [5 feet] per second). ν Moderate (1 to 1.5 meters [3 to 5 feet] per second). ν Slow (less than 1 meter [3 feet] per second).

13-19. Individuals should look upstream for obstacles, and pick up a good athletic stance, angling their body slightly perpendicular to the current. Adjust to a more parallel stance and lean upstream if the current is stronger.

13-20. Pick a location slightly downstream to the Soldier’s position. Traveling at 90° causes Soldiers to fight the current rather than work with the flow of water as much as possible. Always lead off with the downstream foot and take small steps while keeping the feet close to the ground. Avoid moving one foot before securing the other foot, and do not cross legs. This will decrease the likelihood of moving water throwing the Soldier off balance. Additionally, it will allow the Soldier to explore the riverbed for obstacles such as holes, rocks, shoals, or debris for optimal management. If a sizeable rock is found, Soldiers should always step on the upstream side of it. Water cresting the top and sides of rocks picks up speed, digging around and on the downstream side. The integrity of these rocks is unknown and could roll downstream at any time.

13-21. For added stability, using a third contact point is encouraged. A long stick or staff, ice axe, or tree limb could be used. By placing the end of the third point as upstream as possible, Soldiers can create a tripod, while exercising a body position described above to create a streamlined signature. The third point can be useful as a probe, searching for obstacles and depth.

{{img:0}}

sections.heading: Mountain Stream Crossing: TEAM CROSSINGS
sections.body:
13-22. When the water level begins to reach thigh deep, or anytime the current is too swift for personnel to safely perform an individual crossing, a team crossing may be used. With each of these methods, have a leader call each step. One advantage to the team crossing is reduced exposure time for higher concentration of personnel, and there is no equipment to recover once Soldiers have performed the crossing. Disadvantages for all team crossings include a lack of interval for free movement and negotiation of riverbed makeup.

Additionally, the close concentration of personnel makes them an easy target for direct or indirect enemy fires. The speed at which Soldiers can move fire teams and squads is that of a singular unit.
