images.caption: Figure 13-2. Chain method for stream crossing

sections.heading: Mountain Stream Crossing: CHAIN CROSSING (CONGA VARIATION)

images.caption: Figure 13-3. Insert side view, top view, and traveling

sections.heading: Mountain Stream Crossing: WEDGE OR DIAMOND TEAM CROSSING
sections.body: 13-25. Three or more individuals form a wedge, with the largest individual upstream to break the current for the group. Cross arms behind the back or rucksack and grasp the upstream individual, developing structured support. Subsequent personnel widen the wedge with smaller personnel or casualties filling the middle portion. Maintain an interval that supports free movement without tripping on other personnel. The wedge formed has the added support of each other. Move across the stream using most of the same principles as for individual crossings but all facing upstream. The team still moves at a slight downstream angle, stepping off with the downstream foot in the lead stepping together as one unit. If the formation begins to degrade, avoid trying to excessively hang onto personnel who have lost control. The alternative of swimming is the safest in that scenario.

sections.heading: Mountain Stream Crossing: BELAYED CROSSINGS
sections.body:
13-26. Certain conditions may require using a rope system to aid in crossing or even keep Soldiers from being exposed to water. When the depth begins to approach knee to waist level and the current is strong enough to potentially knock a Soldier off balance, then using a handline (one rope bridge with belay line) could be appropriate. This is the safest form of crossing simply because Soldiers have direct influence from either riverbank.

13-27. Crossing on a handline will still require everyone to enter the water. In a case where water and air temperature significantly increase the risk of hypothermia, artificial height or other considerations may need to be implemented. Joining two or more ropes will only be possible for a handline. The maximum distance a one-rope bridge is capable of spanning is about one-half to two-thirds the length of the rope in use.

13-28. An advantage of using a belayed crossing is the safety aspect. If individual control is lost, personnel can be pulled to the unloading bank by those belaying. Disadvantages of this technique are the time required for preparation, the number of available anchors, and the time dedicated to recovering the crossing site.

sections.heading: Mountain Stream Crossing: ESTABLISHING THE FAR ANCHOR
sections.body:
13-29. Whether a handline or rope bridge (see chapter 16) is to be installed, someone must cross the stream with one end of the rope and anchor it on the far side. The most capable and strongest swimmer in the party should perform this duty. Swimmers should be belayed across for their own safety. The belay position should be placed as far above the crossing as possible. If the current is too strong for individuals, they will pendulum back to the near bank. Rescuers should be poised on the near bank at points where individuals will pendulum back, should they fail to reach the far bank. The initial crossing site should be free of obstacles that would snag the rope and prevent the pendulum from going back to the bank for an easy recovery.

13-30. Individuals may attach the belay rope to their seat harness or a swami belt with a carabiner. They should never tie directly into the rope when being belayed for a stream crossing. If swimmers are swept away and become tangled, they must be able to release themselves quickly from the rope and swim to shore as best they can. Individuals may also choose to tie a fixed loop into the end of the belay rope and hang on to it, where they can immediately release it in an emergency.

13-31. Anytime a crossing site must be used where swimmers may encounter problems getting to the far bank, they should wear a life vest or other personal flotation device (PFD). If swimmers must release the rope at any time, they will have to rely on their own water survival skills and swimming ability to get to shore. A PFD greatly increases personal safety. A PFD may also be used by the last individuals across, as they will release the rope from the anchor and be belayed across as the first individual.

sections.heading: Mountain Stream Crossing: INSTALLATION OF A HANDLINE
sections.body:
13-32. If it is possible to use a rope high enough above the water to enable Soldiers to perform a dry crossing, then a rope bridge should be installed as such. If this is impossible, and the rope must be installed to assist in a wet crossing, then it should be installed as a handline. (See figure 13-4.)

13-33. The far anchor should be downstream from the near anchor so that the rope will run at an angle downstream from the near anchor, about 30° to 45°, rather than straight across the stream. Here again, it is easier to move with the current as opposed to directly across or against it.

13-34. The rope may be anchored immediately on the far bank, pulled tight, and anchored on the near bank.

If a tighter rope is required, the handline may be installed with a transport tightening system. (See chapter 16.)

13-35. A second climbing rope is used as a belay. (See figure 13-5, page 330.) One end of the belay rope will be on the near bank and the other end on the far bank. It should be sent across with the strong swimmer. An appropriate knot is tied into the middle of the belay rope to form two fixed loops. Each loop is approximately 6-inches long. One loop is connected to the handline with a carabiner and individuals crossing connect one loop to themselves. The loops are short enough so individuals are always within arm’s reach of the handline should they slip and let go. Individuals are belayed from both the near and far banks. If a mishap should occur, the individual can be retrieved from either shore, whichever appears easiest. The belay on the opposite shore can be released, allowing the individual to pendulum to the bank. It is important not to anchor or tie the belay rope to the belayer so that it may be released quickly if necessary.

sections.heading: Mountain Stream Crossing: MOVEMENT

images.caption: Figure 13-5. Moving on handline with belay

sections.heading: Mountain Stream Crossing: SWIMMING
sections.body:
13-38. Soldiers may find themselves alone and have no choice but to swim across, or they may find themselves suddenly plunged into a swift river or rapids. Soldiers should consider the following actions if Soldiers are in a situation that forces them to swim during a crossing:

Immediately strip away gear or clothing that restricts free movement and increases their signature.

Instead of fighting the current, work with the flow of water to get to a dry location downstream. It is often easier to negotiate hazards and see where Soldiers are going if they face downstream and fan the hands alongside the body to add buoyancy. They should use their hands to also fend off submerged rocks and position their feet as a shock absorber to shove off unseen or hidden obstacles.

- Keep the head above water to identify obstacles or debris that Soldiers may impact. Take the

opportunity to breathe between breaks if waves begin to rise over Soldiers’ heads.

- Avoid backwater eddies, bubbly water, water churning upwards, and converging currents. All these

hazards have the potential to create unpredictable buoyancy and possibly undertow.

If the shore is too difficult to reach, seek out the closest and safest spot, such as a sandbar, to get out of the water as quickly as possible. Hypothermia will set in quickly in colder waters.

sections.heading: Mountain Stream Crossing: SECTION III – ADDITIONAL CONSIDERATIONS AND HAZARDS
sections.body: 13-39. River and stream crossings present one of the most hazardous situations faced by military mountaineers. Substantial experience is necessary to properly evaluate and mitigate swift water hazards.

sections.heading: Mountain Stream Crossing: SAFETY GUIDELINES FOR RIVER AND STREAM CROSSINGS
sections.body:
13-40. The following safety procedures are minimum guidelines that should be followed when conducting a river or stream crossing:

- All weak swimmers should be identified before a crossing so that stronger swimmers may assist in

crossing.

- Not every river or stream can be crossed safely. If it is possible, cross at a different time or place,

use a different technique, or choose another route.

The technique used is directly dependent upon water depth, speed of the current, stream bottom configuration, width of the stream, and individual experience.

The safest methods of crossing in the water are always with the use of a handline or rope bridge.

If the installation of a handline or rope bridge becomes too difficult at a given crossing site, then that site should be considered too hazardous and another site selected.

- A lookout should be posted 50 to 100 meters upstream to watch for any obstacles that may be carried

downstream and interfere with the crossing.

- When conducting individual crossings (those without a handline or rope bridge), spotters or security should be posted downstream with poles or ropes prepared to throw, for assistance or rescue. Medical personnel should be prepared for cases of hypothermia.

- When the unit knows a rope installation is required for crossing, at least two life vests or other PFDs should be on hand. These PFDs provide additional safety for the strong swimmer who must establish the far anchor and the last individual across who retrieves the system.

sections.heading: Mountain Stream Crossing: WATER SURFACE CLUES
sections.body:
13-41. Observing and analyzing the top of the water can give military mountaineers an indication of what to expect beneath the surface. Water is not often clear enough to see all the hazards that could make the crossing difficult or have adverse effects on personnel attempting to cross. The following are common clues that can provide ideas of what lies beneath the surface.

Riffles or ripples—if they are lined up, there are likely one or several rocks that form a line. In shallower water, it could mean a stable, rocky riverbed.

- Holes, souse holes, or keepers—depressions that can form from water moving around an obstacle. The rise and drop on the surface can be visibly seen. Avoid stepping here as these rises and drops could suction Soldiers’ feet and debris can fall. Convergences and their depth—can increase the force the water has on someone attempting to cross. Eddy or back eddy—swirling of water and the reverse current created when water flows over or around an object or terrain. The consistency of a current is very unpredictable.

documents.title: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation (TC 3-97.61 Ch. 15)

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation
sections.body:
**Chapter 15**

A unit’s capability to conduct mountain rescue and evacuation is a critical part of mountain operations. Swift and efficient rescue can mean the difference between success and failure of a mission or even the survival of a casualty. In mountainous terrain, even relatively minor injuries may require evacuation. The type of injury, distance to be moved, terrain, training level of the team, and litter capabilities determine the evacuation technique chosen. Air evacuation is preferred. However, the weather, tactical situation, or operational ceiling of the aircraft may make this impossible. Therefore, it is imperative that all personnel are trained in mountain evacuation techniques and are self-sufficient. Casualties should be triaged before evacuation.

The most experienced medical personnel available perform triage (physician, physician’s assistant, or medic).

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: SECTION I – RESCUE OPERATIONS
sections.body:
15-1. Every commander should have a MEDEVAC plan before undertaking an operation. This plan should have dedicated assets (primary, alternate, contingency, and emergency) in place so as not to rely on a single evacuation platform or method. Rotary-wing aircraft may be available to remove casualties from cliffs or inaccessible sites and to quickly transport casualties to a medical treatment facility. However, high altitudes and gusting winds reduce the ability of fixed-wing or rotary-wing aircraft to assist in operations. Therefore, relying solely on aircraft or specialized equipment is a poor substitute for careful planning.

15-2. The two types of rescue operations encountered by units operating in mountainous environments are deliberate and improvised.

**Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: DELIBERATE**

15-3. Deliberate rescue is when the mission objective itself is a rescue operation, thus allowing time for focused planning and the use of specialized rescue specific equipment.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: IMPROVISED
sections.body: 15-4. Improvised rescue situations are encountered when a casualty is sustained during normal operations and conducting a rescue was not the intended objective. Even improvised rescue operations should be practiced and rehearsed to minimize the negative effects on mission capability. All operations should have a CASEVAC plan developed before an emergency arises (plan for the worst and hope for the best). Ensure that the MEDEVAC plan is well thought out and comprehensive. These plans must be understood by all who may be involved in a potential rescue.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: PLANNING
sections.body:
15-5. The rescue tasks must be identified by obtaining the following information:

Terrain features and with respect to the location of the casualties.

Tactical situation.

- Number of casualties by precedence (urgent, priority, routine, convenience).

- Number of casualties by type (litter or ambulatory) and the nature of their injuries.

- Any assets available to aid in security, rescue, treatment, and evacuation.

- Additional personnel or equipment required for the rescue operation.

- Any circumstances that may require specialized skills.

- Weather conditions.

- Difficulty of the terrain.

Time available.

If treatment can be provided at the scene or if the casualty requires movement to a safer location.

15-6. Route selection when planning mountain CASEVAC often depends upon technical capabilities. In some cases, trained personnel and equipment available for low- or high-angle rescue may allow for safer, less physically demanding operations. A lack of these resources and capabilities may require traveling longer distances around steeper terrain, greatly increasing the burden on rescuers.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: CONSIDERATIONS
sections.body:
15-7. Time considerations can cause a leader to compromise planning stages or treatment (beyond first aid).

Make a realistic estimate of time available as quickly as possible to determine the action time remaining. The key elements are the casualty’s condition and ability to endure the environment. Time available is a balance between these conditions and the resources and personnel available.

15-8. There are many additional considerations for the rescue team during deliberate rescue:

Typically, team members must distribute and carry all equipment, including hot food and drinks, stoves, sleeping bags, bivouac equipment, warm clothes, ropes, and stretchers.

Evacuation routes often require extensive preparation and can involve establishing anchor points, belays, fixed ropes, lowers, and raises.

- Altitude and visibility can greatly affect the team as well as the casualty. Maximum use of secure,

reliable trails or roads is essential.

Protection from the elements, such as blankets, tarps, warming layers and rain gear, can be vital.

Even a mild rain can complicate an otherwise simple rescue. In higher altitudes, extreme cold or strong winds can greatly increase the rescue’s time and complexity.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: GENERAL STEPS
sections.body:
15-9. Regardless of whether a rescue is deliberate or improvised, the following steps must be taken upon arrival at the rescue site to accomplish a safe and efficient rescue operation:

- Assume command—one person and one person only is in charge.

Scene safety—prevent further injuries to the casualty and to others. Explore all options for casualty access prior to committing to one. Use reasonable care in reaching the casualty. Rescuers must not become casualties.

Immediately ensure the casualty has an open airway, control serious bleeding, and protect the casualty from further harm and from environmental hazards. If the casualty is unconscious, continually monitor for a pulse.

- Do not move the casualty until determining the extent of injuries unless necessary to prevent further

injury or if the casualty is in a dangerous or exposed location.

- Do nothing more until the situation has been thoroughly considered. Resist the urge for action. Speed is less important than correct actions and decision making. The decisions made on scene drive the rest of the rescue (for example, casualty rigging, packaging, route selection, anchors, and rope systems).

- Decide whether to evacuate with available resources or to send or call for help. Speed in getting to the next level of care must be balanced against the probability of further injury. This is especially crucial if working with inexperienced personnel, insufficient equipment, or terrain or weather hazards.

- When the evacuation route is long and arduous, a series of litter relay points or stations should be established, if possible. These help to manage the welfare of both the casualty and the rescue team. These stations should be staffed with the medical personnel and equipment necessary to provide proper treatment.

- Helicopters or heated vehicles, if available, should be used for evacuation. While the use of aircraft or vehicles is preferred and can expedite a rescue operation, evacuation of a seriously wounded Soldier should never be delayed awaiting aircraft, vehicle, or a change in weather.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: SPECIALIZED TRAINING
sections.body:
15-10. Rescue team members must receive basic instruction in military mountaineering and first aid, prior to any training and rehearsals for mountain rescue and evacuation. Individual mobility skills, knowledge of knots and basic rope systems, and the ability to sustain and protect themselves from the environment are

essential. Once formal evacuation training has been received, proficiency can be maintained by periodic integration with other concurrent training exercises. Scenarios that require simple casualty movement techniques, with and without litters, as well as low-angle slope evacuations (see section II) can easily be created. Scenarios are added when time becomes available during or following other training exercises. These opportunities allow commanders to quickly evaluate a unit’s preparedness to carry out basic rescues if needed, refresh level 1 skills, and help to reinforce unit teamwork and problem solving. Basic military mountaineers, at a minimum, should oversee this training. Medical personnel should be present. Rescues in complex 4th- and 5th-class terrain, whether real or simulated, require advanced-level training and skills, and they must be led by level 2 and level 3 mountaineers.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: PROLONGED FIELD CARE
sections.body:
15-11. The mountain environment is defined by austere and remote conditions. This environment, combined with the difficulty of patient movement, creates situations that can extend patient management over many hours or days. Prolonged field care is the continued delivery of medical care prior to patient movement beyond the holding capability of that role of care (JP 4-02).

15-12. Medical personnel with standard training may be required to perform beyond their skillset. Specific training should be conducted to prepare medical and nonmedical personnel for prolonged field care situations.

Tactical combat casualty care uses protocols aimed primarily at preventing mortality in the first few hours of treatment, prior to arrival at surgical resuscitative care. However, patients in the mountains lacking fast and immediate evacuation are often at risk for complications, such as sepsis, multi-organ system failure, respiratory compromise, and other serious conditions. Prolonged field care begins with the sound principles of tactical combat casualty care, but when care is extended over hours or days, treatment must continuously be re-evaluated. Diligence is necessary to minimize the effect of potentially harmful interventions and to prevent, recognize, and treat conditions that may develop over time.

15-13. Critical patients ultimately require care in a hospital with surgery, blood products, an intensive care unit, and advanced imaging. A combination of rescue skills training and prolonged field care skills are necessary to make this possible.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: SECTION II – CASUALTY MOVEMENT TECHNIQUES
sections.body: 15-14. Casualties in the mountains can be moved and transported in a variety of ways, from simple manual field carries to high-angle evacuations using litters and complex rope systems. The type of injury, distance to be moved, time available, and resources will determine the best technique for a given situation.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: MOVING CASUALTIES WITHOUT LITTERS
sections.body:
15-15. There are varieties of circumstances where casualties may move, be moved, or be carried without the use of litters. This could be a result of sustaining relatively minor injuries, not having a litter available, or not having the available personnel for litter transport. Alternatively, these could involve moving a casualty in technical terrain that is not suited for transport in a litter. If casualties are able, they can walk, with one or more rescuers walking alongside, to provide physical support. A rescuer close behind can help in difficult terrain. Have team members ahead to select the easiest route and remove loose branches and other obstacles.

Ski poles may be helpful if they are available. In situations where the casualty cannot walk, simple techniques described in the Soldier’s Manual of Common Tasks (fireman’s carry, two-hand, four-hand, saddleback, piggyback, pistol belt, and poncho litter) may be useful. However, rugged mountainous terrain often demands other techniques. The most basic one-man carries include the webbing or rope carry, the rope coil carry, and the rucksack carry.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: NYLON WEBBING OR ROPE CARRY
sections.body:
15-16. A 4.5-meter piece of webbing or rope can be used to improvise a buddy carry system. (See figure 15-1, page 356.) Place the middle of the webbing around the casualty’s back and under the shoulders, crossing in front of the chest. Place the ends over the carrier’s shoulders (from back to front). Bring the ends alongside the carrier’s ribs, through the casualty’s crotch, and around the outside of the casualty’s thighs. The carrier then ties the ends of the webbing together around the waste with a square knot.

{{img:0}}

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: ROPE COIL CARRY
sections.body: 15-17. A dynamic or static rope can also be used as an improvised buddy carry system. (See figure 15-2.) Coil the length of rope using the mountain coil technique, sizing the loops to fit from the casualty’s armpits to crotch, and then separate the coil in half to form a pair of loops. Place the casualty’s legs through the loops and slip the upper part of the loops over the carrier’s shoulders. A short piece of webbing can be used to tie these loops together.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: RUCKSACK CARRY
sections.body:
{{img:0}}

15-18. The rucksack carry is another method of back carry. Make slits in the sides of a large rucksack so the casualty can step into it as though it were a pair of shorts. Then the carrier wears the backpack as usual. This requires the contents of the carrier’s pack to be carried by another Soldier.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: TANDEM RAPPEL
sections.body:
15-19. Rappelling with a casualty is not often the first choice in rescue. It is typically preferable to lower a casualty with a rescuer during descents because it allows the rescuer to focus on controlling the casualty rather than having to control both the casualty and a rappel. However, in the case of a sturdy, conscious patient with nonlife-threatening injuries, it is possible to rappel together with a rescuer. To do this, a rappel extension can be created using a 48-inch sling or cordelette as shown below to allow both the casualty and rescuer to rappel from the same device but slightly offset from one another. (See figure 15-3, page 358.) The rescuer must add an autoblock back up behind the device.

{{img:0}}

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: ROPED MOVEMENTS
sections.body: 15-20. Casualties can also be placed in a seat or improvised harness and lowered or hauled through steep terrain using the techniques described in chapter 12. This may be done with ambulatory patients or may be necessary in situations where an injured Soldier must be moved from a cliff to an alternate location where packaging in a litter is more easily accomplished. This may require considerable assistance from rescuers or other Soldiers. It should only be attempted when necessary and after any immediate life-threatening injuries have been treated. Remember the more complex the technical rope systems become, the more time consuming they tend to be, increasing exposure and vulnerability to enemy attack.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: MOVING CASUALTIES IN LITTERS
sections.body: 15-21. Usually, casualties with significant injuries in the mountains need to be evacuated with the use of a litter. Several types of litters are available for transporting casualties in rough terrain.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: MANUFACTURED LITTERS
sections.body:
15-22. The following litters are readily available to mountaineering units:

The poleless, nonrigid litter is lightweight and readily available but is the least favored litter. It does little to protect the patient’s injuries and is not appropriate for attachment to any rope system.

The standard collapsible litter is readily available in all units and may be rigged for movement over rough mountainous terrain. However, it is not suitable for carry as a contingency litter due to its bulk and weight.

- A rigid, metal-framed, basket-style litter that is rated for hoist operations is very well-suited for moving casualties through mountainous environments. These litters provide excellent patient protection and spinal immobilization, and when rigged properly, can readily attach to a variety of technical rope systems. The drawbacks to this type of litter are that it is heavy and is not designed to slide over surfaces. A single-wheel attachment is available, which vastly increases the efficiency of movement over moderate terrain but comes at the cost of an even greater weight to be carried. The patient rescue and recovery collapsible litter system is a lightweight, semirigid, rollout plastic litter that can also be rigged to meet rating requirements for hoist operations. The most commonly issued and used version in mountaineering is the rescue litter, which provides excellent patient support and protection. This is the preferred litter for mountain operations due to its versatility and relatively low weight. However, it is not a spinal immobilization device. A backboard must be used with this system for patients who have injuries to the shoulder area. This system will accommodate long and short backboards, scoop stretchers, and most other immobilization equipment.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: IMPROVISED LITTERS
sections.body:
15-23. Litters can be improvised in the field using several techniques, but all of them require construction materials and time, generally offer less patient protection, and are more prone to breakage.

15-24. Litters can be made by securing poles inside blankets, tarps, ponchos, jackets, shirts, sacks, or bags.

Poles can be improvised from strong branches, tent supports, skis, and other similar items.

15-25. If poles cannot be found, a large item, such as a blanket, can be rolled from both sides toward the center. Then the rolls can be used to obtain a firm grip to carry the casualty. If a poncho is used, the hood must be up and under the victim, not dragging on the ground.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: PATIENT PACKAGING
sections.body:
15-26. Casualties must be packaged and secured to litters before movement in rough terrain. Proper packaging should achieve stabilization, immobilization, protection from hypothermia, and preparation for transport. Physically strapping a person into a litter is relatively easy but making it comfortable and effective can be a challenge. The needs of litter bound casualties are great and should not be overlooked or underestimated. The decisions made during initial packaging will affect the physical and mental outcomes for the casualty in the end.

15-27. The rescuer’s goals are as follows:

Package the casualty to avoid causing additional injury.

Ensure the casualty’s comfort and warmth with focus on preventing hypothermia.

Immobilize the casualty’s entire body in such a way as to allow continued assessment during transport.

Package the casualty neatly so that the litter can be moved easily and safely.

Ensure that casualties are safe during transport by securing them within the litter and belaying the litter as necessary.

15-28. Rescuers follow the same basic principles of the cold-weather clothing system to create a hypothermia wrap (hypo-wrap). The fundamental goal is to reduce heat loss. The outermost layer should be a VB to protect the casualty and the insulating layers from the environment. Use a ground pad to protect against conductive heat loss using a closed cell or inflatable foam pad. A closed-cell foam sleep pad is preferable because it will not rupture, and it can be cut into pieces for additional medical treatments (such as splints and neck braces).

Begin layering with available insulating materials. The casualty’s equipment should be used first before sacrificing clothing or sleep systems from non-injured Soldiers. Rescuers put the casualty into the wrap and place additional layers of insulation on top of the casualty.

15-29. Consider protecting the insulating layers from casualties themselves if there is a possibility they could become incontinent. A trash bag or waterproof bag with leg holes cut in it can be filled with socks or T-shirts to form a diaper. Wrap the casualty as completely as possible, leaving only necessary areas exposed. When available, hot water bottles should be added and placed by the casualty’s axillary areas (armpits, groin) and the neck to provide active rewarming.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: MOVEMENT TECHNIQUES
sections.body:
15-30. ATP 4-02.13 covers general principles of handling and moving with litters—principles that apply in all terrain. However, in rugged mountainous terrain, teams must often move considerably slower. Extensive personnel may be required to ensure adequate rest and safety. Advanced teams may be useful for route selection and clearing.

15-31. For longer movements, it can be useful to add slings or cordelettes to the litter rim or handles for each litter bearer. These slings can be passed over the shoulders to the opposite hand, allowing each bearer to push down with the hand opposite the litter. This can help to reduce strain on the arm and hand carrying the litter, as well as providing some height adjustment.

15-32. In severely uneven terrain, such as talus or boulder fields, the pass-through technique can make movement safer for both the casualty and rescuers, provided extra personnel are available. To conduct the pass-through technique, simply have extra litter bearers take up static positions in the terrain ahead of the litter and as close to one another as possible. The litter is then passed forward into the hands of the extra litter bearers. As soon as litter bearers in the rear become obsolete, they move around and take up a new position further ahead in the direction of travel. They then wait until the litter reaches them and repeat the technique.

This allows rescuers to remain still as the litter is transported, taking advantage of secure footing and stable positions. In this way, the litter is less likely to be dropped and litter bearers are less likely to sustain an injury attempting to move and carry the heavy load at the same time.

15-33. If a litter can be dragged, attaching ropes may make doing so easier and more controllable. Ropes can be attached to the front of the litter for dragging purposes as well as to the rear of the litter for use with a brakeman to slow the speed of the litter on gentle descents. This technique can speed up evacuation in conditions that allow for it, such as snow-covered terrain. (See figure 15-4.)

15-34. On flat or low-angle snow-covered terrain, two ropes can be attached to the corners of the litter with girth hitches to allow up to four Soldiers to pull, brake, and steer the litter. This enables moving up, down, and traversing slopes with better control to prevent the litter from tipping over.

{{img:0}}

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: LOW-ANGLE RESCUE
sections.body: 15-35. Low-angle rescue can generally be categorized by roped litter evacuations on low to moderately steep slopes where much of the weight of the casualty and rescuer is still supported by the ground. In this terrain, the litter slides along the slope, either up or down, depending on the direction of travel. The rope pathway should be cleared prior to casualty movement. All precautions must be taken to keep the litter within the fall line of gravity to eliminate pendulum swings. In all situations, the rescue team should strive to solve the terrain problem safely with the least technical solution.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: ROPE ATTACHMENT

images.caption: Figure 15-5. Litter rigged for vertical orientation
Figure 15-6. Basket litter rigged for vertical orientation

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: BELAYS
sections.body: 15-39. In some situations, the rescue rope can be used to simply provide a tight belay for the casualty while litter teams carry a litter up or down slopes. Many of the various belay techniques described in chapter 10 are appropriate for this; however, the terrain must be gentle enough that there is no falling hazard to members of the litter team.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: ATTENDANTS
sections.body:
15-40. In steeper terrain where lowering or raising the litter from above is necessary, there is often a falling hazard for the litter team. If rescuers cannot safely walk beside the litter, it is typically advisable to use a single rescuer attached to the system as an attendant. This attendant’s primary responsibility is to ensure the litter and casualty do not roll over, become hung up on terrain obstacles, or create slack in the system.

15-41. One technique is to attach the rescue rope to the litter head using a bowline with a tail that is long enough to reach the bottom of the litter when stretched out. The long tail is then be used by a litter attendant as an attachment point to the system in situations where it is necessary. (See figure 15-7.) This can also be achieved using a figure eight on a bight with enough rope behind the knot to extend this distance.

15-42. The attendant can attach directly into the end of this rope with another figure eight on a bight attached to a locking carabiner in the harness or by tying directly in with a rerouted figure eight. An autoblock or prusik can also be attached to this strand of rope to allow the attendant to adjust position in relation to the litter and hang completely from the system. Occasionally but less often, two attendants may be required to manage the litter.

15-43. These methods use some of the rope that is available for the rescue. In cases where the length of available rope is limited, it may be prudent to improvise the attendant’s attachment using other materials, such as a cordelette.

{{img:0}}

images.caption: Figure 15-7. Litter rigged for lowering with long-tailed bowline and attendant attached

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: LOWERING
sections.body:
15-44. The litter and attendant can be lowered using various lowering techniques described in chapter 12.

Select or construct extremely solid anchors, tie off the end of the rope to close the system, and apply appropriate hands-free backups. The rope pathway should be cleared prior to casualty movement, and all precautions must be taken to keep the litter within the fall line of gravity to eliminate pendulum swings. A Soldier secured safely near the edge can often be helpful to relay commands and help control the speed of the lower. Avoid rope pathways with sharp rock edges or loose terrain with rockfall potential.

15-45. If it is necessary to lower the litter and attendant multiple rope lengths, multiple anchor stations and lowering teams may be required to achieve this. Complex situations such as this require excellent leadership, terrain assessment, and communication.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: RAISING
sections.body: 15-46. The litter and attendant can be raised through steep terrain using the various hauling techniques described in chapter 12. This could be done by a hauling team from above using main force or by creating MA using one of the systems previously described. If using main force, a prusik or other friction hitch should be attached to the rope and anchored as a progress capture. An additional member on the haul team must be dedicated to managing the prusik during this method. If using MA, the hauling team must pull slow and steady and should be extremely aware of the loss of feel for the load. In either case, the rope pathway should be cleared prior to casualty movement, and all precautions must be taken to keep the litter within the fall line of gravity to eliminate pendulum swings. A Soldier secured safely near the edge can often be helpful to relay commands and help control the speed of the haul. Avoid hauling in terrain with sharp rock edges or loose terrain with rockfall potential.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: HIGH-ANGLE RESCUE
sections.body:
15-47. High-angle rescue generally refers to roped evacuations down steep cliffs and 5th-class terrain.

High-angle rescue requires formal training, experience, excellent judgement, and good technical problem-solving skills. It often requires a substantial amount of time. Only level 2 and 3 military mountaineers should only conduct high-angle rescue, when necessary. There are often many variables involved in high-angle rescue, and thus, there is no prescriptive set way to deal with the many challenges that can be encountered. Because a combination of skills and techniques may ultimately be required, including climbing techniques, belays, rappels, hauling and lowering methods, or even the use of high lines, a comprehensive focus is well beyond the scope of this training circular. Rather, this section will focus on some of the fundamental principles and commonly used tools and techniques.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: LITTER RIGGING
sections.body: 15-48. Whether a rescue litter or a rigid metal basket is used for a high-angle evacuation, the rigging is similar. The litter can be rigged for horizontal orientation, like a helicopter hoist configuration, or it can be rigged for a vertical orientation the same as described for lower-angle evacuations. In many cases, it is ideal to package the casualty in a manufactured or improvised harness. This allows the harness to connect to the rope system independently of the attachment to the litter itself. This can also be achieved with webbing using a variety of techniques.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: Horizontal Orientation

images.caption: Figure 15-8. Litter rigged horizontal orientation with hoist straps
Figure 15-9. Basket litter rigged for horizontal orientation

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: Vertical Orientation
sections.body:
15-50. Vertical litter orientation is often preferred as it can make for a simpler and more fluid edge transition.

It is also lower profile, protects the patient better from rockfall and other hazards, and does not require a change in rope attachment point when transitioning to or from low-angle terrain. However, this method can be unsuitable for casualties with spinal, pelvic, and some lower leg injuries and requires securing the patient in such a way to minimize movement in the litter once evacuation begins.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: ROPE SELECTION
sections.body:
15-51. Rope rescue systems should meet the industry standard 10:1 static system safety factor (SSSF).

Calculate the SSSF by first determining the force created by the rescue load. Each person attached to the system is estimated to create 1 kN. Therefore, one casualty and one rescuer are estimated to be a 2-kN load.

For a 2-kN load, all components of the rescue system must be rated to 20-kN breaking strength to meet the 10:1 SSSF requirement. In this case, ropes would require a minimum breaking strength of around 30 kN to account for an estimated 1/3 strength loss when knots are tied into the rope. Most static kernmantle ropes 11 mm in diameter meet this 30 kN threshold. However, for mountain rescue operations, it is much more practical to use lighter weight ropes that can more easily be carried, allow for faster response times, and function better with other components of the mountaineering kits. These may have MBSs that are a little less than 30 kN, but the advantages often outweigh the risks of encroaching on the very robust 10:1 SSSF. More important than the strength of a thinner diameter rope, users must be cognizant of edge abrasion issues. These ropes should be static (low stretch) and should have a minimum diameter of 9.5 mm and a minimum breaking strength of 26 kN.

15-52. Rescues can be carried out using single or tandem rope systems.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: Single Rope
sections.body:
15-53. Single rope technique, much like that described for use with low-angle rescue, is typically simpler to construct and operate, and generally requires less equipment overall. However, it does not include redundancy for system or rope failure. Equipment breakage or human error can have catastrophic results.

Consider using this technique only when there is no prominent edge transition, no sharp rock edges on the pitch, and time and resources are limited.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: Tandem Rope
sections.body:
15-54. Tandem rope technique is more complex and time consuming, and gear intensive to construct.

However, it has the added benefit of built-in redundancy against system or rope failure or human errors in rigging and operation. Consider tandem rope systems when there are prominent or difficult edge transitions due to the potential for high-peak forces in the event of failure, sharp rock edges, or when there is limited team experience regarding the rigging of anchors and lowering or belay systems.

15-55. Tandem rope technique uses two separate ropes referred to as the main line and the belay line. Each rope system requires a separate anchor. The main line is used to haul or lower the litter, and the belay line is there in case of main line failure.

15-56. The two ropes are connected to the litter attachment point with interlocking long tailed bowlines. (See figure 15-10.) The tail or free end of each bowline is used as a secondary attachment point for the patient and the litter attendant.

{{img:0}}

15-57. The main line is often routed through a high directional or A-frame near the top edge of the cliff to reduce friction at the edge, and to make the transition over the edge easier. (See figure 15-11, page 368.)

{{img:1}}

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: LOWERING
sections.body: 15-58. Sites suitable for lowering should have solid anchor points, good loading and unloading platforms, and good clearance for the casualty along the route. Terrain with sharp rock edges or loose terrain with rockfall potential should be avoided when lowering is necessary. The litter and attendant can be lowered using various lowering techniques described in chapter 12, but techniques that generally provide greater friction are preferred. The end of the rope should be tied off to close the system.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: RAISING
sections.body: 15-59. Sites suitable for hauling should have solid anchor points, good loading and unloading platforms, and good clearance for the casualty along the route. Terrain with sharp rock edges or loose terrain with rockfall potential should be avoided when hauling is necessary. The litter and attendant may be hauled using techniques described in chapter 12. Systems with higher ratios may be necessary, as well as redirection and piggyback techniques.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: BELAY LINE
sections.body:
15-60. While a properly constructed main line and solid anchor system should not fail, there is potential for a severe shock to the system if the attendant slips going over the edge. If such a slip occurs, the shock load will be significant due to the short amount of rope available to absorb the force, and the static nature of all the system components. The separate belay line is also here for this purpose. If a high directional is used, the belay line should not be routed through it. This would cause a greater fall distance before the belay line could catch the load in the event of failure or breakage of the high directional.

15-61. While there are manufactured devices available that meet the criteria for a technical rescue belay, the simplest and most field expedient method is called the tandem prusik belay. Two prusiks, preferably made from 7- or 8-mm nylon static utility cord are tied approximately 2-inches apart on the belay line. The length of the prusik closer to the anchor should be a few inches shorter than the other prusik. These prusiks are then attached to the belay anchor with a locking carabiner. To use the belay, keep an uphill hand on the two prusiks

together and the downhill hand on the downhill side of the rope. Feed rope through the prusiks with a “hitchhikers grip” (thumbs out) and keep a bow of rope approximately 8 to 12 inches of slack between the hands. There should be only a few inches of slack between the downhill hand and the litter. In the event of a blown edge transition or of main line failure, the prusiks will be ripped out of the belayer’s hands and catch the load. Tandem prusiks and belay line are also helpful when transitioning from a lower to a raise or when passing a knot through the lowering system.

**Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: POSITIONS AND RESPONSIBILITIES**

15-62. A high-angle rescue requires a skilled team to be conducted. The following positions are a bare minimum and mandatory for a safe evacuation.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: Team Leader
sections.body:
15-63. The team leader has overall responsibility for the operation. The team leader considers all available options and selects the most appropriate technique for the situation. The team leader makes judgments based on the nature or urgency of the injury, the tactical situation, the nature of the terrain, and the personnel and resources available. The team leader briefs the plan, provides the necessary guidance to the team members, and oversees the operation until complete. The team leader should not handle the main line or the belay, but in short workforce situations, should be found near the edge to assist in communication. The team leader establishes and supervises a formal rigging inspection process, as well as the command and control protocol for all technical operations.

**Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: Belayer**

15-64. The belayer manages the belay ensuring the prusiks do not lock out. Typically, the belayer is responsible for construction and rigging of the belay.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: Main line
sections.body: 15-65. The main line will consist of either a one- or two-person lowering team or a haul team for raises. In the case of teams, only one person should be the spokesperson to keep communications clear. Typically, the main line team is responsible for anchor construction and hauling system rigging.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: Edge Safety
sections.body: 15-66. The edge safety keeps the edge area clean of debris, places edge protection if necessary, and assists the load over the edge during the transition. The edge safety also relays commands between the attendant and the personnel above. During difficult edge transitions, two edge safeties may be used.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: Attendant
sections.body:
15-67. This litter attendant manages the handling of the patient and litter during the technical portion of the rescue. Often the primary focus of the attendant is making sure that the litter is protected and keeping slack out of the system. These often require pulling the litter out away from the terrain for smooth lowers or raises.

This is considerably taxing and may require having an adjustable length attachment to the rope system. The litter attendant should have both primary and secondary attachment points for redundancy. The litter attendant determines and adjusts the rate of litter movement up or down as necessary.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: Inspections
sections.body: 15-68. Units should develop their own deliberate inspection protocols for rescue rope system rigging. At a minimum, rigging for each system component (for example, main, belay, litter) should be inspected systematically as a deliberate step by advanced mountaineers who did not participate in building it.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: Control
sections.body:
15-69. In some cases, to free up the team leader, a separate control person is used for actual commands. This allows the team leader to maintain a broader perspective and continue to think about the next phase or stage

of the operation. The control gives commands to lower or raise the load, especially during the critical edge transition phase.

sections.heading: Mountain Rescue and Evacuation: COMMAND AND CONTROL
sections.body:
15-70. Precise commands and singular control are necessary for safe operations. All commands should originate either with the team leader, control, or, in some cases, the edge safety. A variety of commands can be used but must be short, simple, and clear. Always include the name of the position in the command, such as SLACK ON MAIN or TENSION ON BELAY. Before any lowering or raising operations take place, a roll call is necessary to ensure all personnel are ready. The roll call should start with personnel near or at the edge and work backwards to the main. Once all personnel are ready and checked and the litter and attendant are in position, begin the operation by calling UP ON MAIN or DOWN ON MAIN. Once the litter is moving, the speed can be adjusted, as necessary. To halt all movement, call STOP. All teams continue to act as if the load is on belay until the command OFF BELAY is given.

15-71. Radios are usually necessary to maintain contact with the attendant on the litter. Once the attendant is over the edge, in high winds, yelling is not reliable and produces a sound signature that can travel unpredictable distances in mountainous terrain.

documents.title: Rope Bridges (TC 3-97.61 Ch. 16)

sections.heading: Rope Bridges
sections.body:
**Chapter 16**

Operations in mountainous terrain often encounter obstacles, such as fast flowing water, ravines, or rock fields. Well-trained mountaineers can exploit this terrain with the use of rope bridges and high lines. These allow units to take the terrain out of the equation by using a rope suspended in the air to cross the obstacle. High lines are a type of rope bridge. The two terms are often used synonymously, and the techniques are relatively interchangeable; however, for the purposes of this training circular, we will refer to rope bridges when used for assisting personnel for river crossings and the term “high lines” to denote rope installations used to span longer or higher gaps in terrain.

sections.heading: Rope Bridges: SECTION I – TECHNIQUES
sections.body:
16-1. A rope bridge is a rope tensioned between two anchors and suspended off the ground to assist units with crossing rivers. These are sometimes necessary in situations with swift and dangerous currents or very cold water, where keeping the majority of Soldiers dry is important.

16-2. Rope bridges can pose distinct disadvantages. Though linear in nature, rope bridge crossings in a tactical environment should be considered VDAs. This is because units establishing and using them are fixed and potentially split by the river obstacle for prolonged periods. This can put them at a significant tactical disadvantage. (See ATP 3-21.50 for more VDA-crossing considerations.)

sections.heading: Rope Bridges: CONSTRUCTION
sections.body: 16-3. The rope bridge is constructed using a static rope. The rope is anchored on the far side of the obstacle in the same manner as described for using handlines in paragraphs 13-26 through 13-29, page 327. It is then tensioned and anchored on the near side of the obstacle. A rope bridge may be built many ways depending upon the tactical situation and area to be crossed. However, all rope bridges share common safety principles for construction and use. Rope bridges must be tensioned as low as practical on the anchor while still facilitating suspending loads and off-loading them. The creation of artificial height (covered later) can be used for rope bridges. The type and location of the tensioning system depend on terrain and situation.

sections.heading: Rope Bridges: METHODS OF TENSIONING
sections.body:
16-4. There are multiple ways to apply tension to a rope. The method selected depends on the length of the bridge, equipment available, personnel available, and time. Regardless of the method used, the principle remains the same; apply just enough tension to facilitate ease of crossing through the terrain.

**WARNING:** Ropes must not be overtensioned. An overtensioned rope is in its weakest state, and the system can apply exponential forces during use. Critical failures can occur with overtensioned ropes.

sections.heading: Rope Bridges: HAND TIGHT
sections.body:
16-5. The simplest and least equipment-intensive method is hand tightening the rope. Once Soldiers anchor one side of the rope, they pull the rope as tight as they can. Next, they tie off the rope using one of three methods: mule knot secured with an overhand knot (see figure 16-1), round turn around anchor and two half hitches on a bight, or a high strength tie off (tensionless hitch). (See figure 16-4, page 374.)

Note. Figure 16-2, and figures 16-3 and 16-4, page 374, illustrate the transport tightening system.

16-6. The benefit of hand tensioning the rope is that it is the fastest way to get the rope tight. The limitation is that if the rope bridge span is long, it may not be possible to apply adequate tension to the rope using this method. Adequate tension may require more personnel than units have available.

sections.heading: Rope Bridges: TRANSPORT TIGHTENING SYSTEM

images.caption: Figure 16-2. Mule knot secured with an overhand knot
Figure 16-3. Round turn around anchor and two half hitches on a bight
Figure 16-4. High strength tie off (tensionless hitch)

sections.heading: Rope Bridges: SIMPLE 3:1 TIGHTENING SYSTEM
sections.body:
16-11. The simple 3:1 tightening system is another method for gaining MA (see chapter 12).

16-12. The benefits of the simple 3:1 system are increased efficiency in tensioning, the capability to tension on a smaller platform, and the ability to re-tension due to rope stretch. The drawbacks are increased complexity, time, equipment, and the possibility of overtensioning the rope. The limitations are that the system requires more equipment, is more complex to construct, is easier to overtension and the increased time required to construct.

**WARNING:** No more than four personnel should be used to tighten the rope when a simple 3:1 or a transport tightening system is used to apply tension. Using more personnel can overtighten the rope and bring the rope critically close to failure.

sections.heading: Rope Bridges: REDUNDANCY
sections.body: 16-13. A rope bridge constructed with a single rope has the risk of critical failure due to cutting and lacks redundancy. A redundancy (in rigging) is the condition in which a rope system will not fail as the result of any single component of the system failing. If the risk or critical nature of the load requires an additional level of redundancy, a second rope bridge may be constructed parallel to the first one. Examples of critical loads are a casualty, Soldiers crossing a rope bridge that is high off the ground, and a dry river crossing where a separate belay rope is not used. If two ropes are used, they should be as close as possible so that a single carabiner can be clipped to both lines. An individual would attach to both ropes when crossing, thus having a backup in case of failure. Redundancy is not always necessary or practical but is typically used in training as a risk management tool.

sections.heading: Rope Bridges: METHODS OF CROSSING
sections.body:
16-14. All wet crossing techniques using handlines are covered in chapter 13. Methods of dry crossings using rope bridges is determined by several factors:

The load being transported on the rope bridge (such as personnel, equipment, and litter).

The risk of the terrain (such as fast-moving water and catastrophic falls).

The angle of the rope bridge (such as level, ascending, and descending).

Equipment available (such as extra ropes, harnesses, and rigging equipment).

16-15. Leaders must evaluate the situation and determine the most efficient means of crossing. For example, the method chosen for moving a light element with no sustainment gear across a 10-foot stream is different from the method chosen for moving crew-served weapons across a 50-foot-wide, fast-moving river.

16-16. If Soldiers can transport themselves across, they can choose either the commando crawl or the Tyrolean traverse.

sections.heading: Rope Bridges: COMMANDO CRAWL
sections.body: 16-17. Soldiers lie on top of the rope with a foot hooked on the rope and a knee bent, o positioned nearly in line with the buttocks; the other leg hangs straight to maintain balance. They progress by pulling with their arms. To recover if they fall over, Soldiers hook one leg and the opposite arm over the rope, and then push down with the other hand to regain position.

sections.heading: Rope Bridges: TYROLEAN TRAVERSE
sections.body: 16-18. Soldiers don a harness or tie a field expedient harness and attach a locking carabiner into it, with the nose of the carabiner facing up and away from their body. They then face the rope and clip into the rope bridge. Soldiers rotate under the rope and pull with their hands and arms to make progress. The Tyrolean traverse is the preferred method. If crossing with rucksacks, a carabiner is inserted into the frame and attached to the rope bridge. Soldiers then place one or both legs through the shoulder carrying straps and pull the rucksack across.

sections.heading: Rope Bridges: TAGLINES
sections.body:
16-19. Heavy equipment will require the use of a tagline. A tagline is used to pull objects from the near side to the far side. An additional rope is brought across the rope bridge and anchored to the far side. The other end is anchored on the near side. All the slack is pulled to the near side, and a figure eight on a bight knot is tied at the loading platform. A carabiner is inserted into the loop and clipped onto the rope bridge.

16-20. If the rope bridge is longer than half a rope length, two separate ropes are required to create a tagline.

One end of the far-side tagline is brought across the obstacle and anchored to the far side. The other end is secured to a carabiner. One end of the near side tagline is secured at the near side, and the other end is secured into the same carabiner as the far-side tagline. That carabiner is then placed onto the rope bridge.

16-21. If the rope bridge is descending (the far-side anchor is significantly lower than the near side), a belay may need to be added to the tagline system. The tagline attached to the near side will be converted into a belay (see chapter 10) to allow for a controlled movement across and down the rope bridge.

sections.heading: Rope Bridges: EQUIPMENT RIGGING
sections.body:
16-22. Any special equipment, such as crew-served weapons, ammunition, or supplies, must be rigged for movement across the rope bridge. A unit SOP may dictate the rigging of these items, but many expedient methods exist. The rigging should use various items that would be readily available to a deployed unit. Some of these items include tubular nylon webbing, cordage (various sizes), and carabiners.

16-23. Equipment that can be bundled together, such as rucksacks, should be Bundles can be created with a cordelette. If there are insufficient personnel on the far side to lift the bundle for unloading, a releasable Munter mule can be utilized at the point of attachment to the tagline.

16-24. Litters can be transported across a rope bridge if there is a secure means of attaching the litter to the rope, such as the rescue litter with its horizontal lift straps. The carabiner of the tagline will remain on the rope bridge. On each side of this carabiner, using the hauling line tie a middle-of-the-rope clove hitch around the carabiners of both horizontal lift straps of the litter. Remove the slack between the carabiners. Then place the carabiners in each of the lift straps onto the rope bridge. (See figure 16-5.) The same technique used for the rucksacks is used to pull the litter across.

sections.heading: Rope Bridges: ARTIFICIAL HEIGHT
sections.body:
{{img:0}}

16-25. Artificial height is often useful or even necessary to raise the height of rope bridges. (See figure 16-6, page 378.) This may be needed when desiring dry river crossings or to better facilitate the loading and unloading of personnel or equipment. Artificial height may be needed on one or both sides of a rope bridge.

16-26. Occasionally, bridge sites may be selected where a tree with a high sturdy limb may be slung with rope or cord. On rock faces, artificial anchors may be constructed in convenient locations. Otherwise, A-frames may need to be constructed.

16-27. A-frames are structures constructed with poles to create artificial height for use with rope bridges.

Two sturdy poles are needed. The exact size of the poles depends on the type of load and location of the installation. The average size A-frame pole should be at least 3 inches in diameter and 9 to 12 feet long.

Three to five 13-foot cordelettes are needed depending on the size of the poles used for the A-frame.

{{img:1}}

images.caption: Figure 16-6. Artificial height (A-frame) used with high line

sections.heading: Rope Bridges: A-FRAME CONSTRUCTION
sections.body:
16-28. There are many acceptable techniques and variations for the construction of A-frames. The general process is described as follows: (See figure 16-7.)

Place two suitable poles with the butt ends flush and mark the desired apex on both poles.

- With a section of rope or cordelette, tie a clove hitch around one of the poles a few inches above the apex marking, leaving about 12 inches of tail to the outside of the poles. (See figure 16-7[A].)

- With the poles side by side, wrap the remaining length of rope horizontally around both poles six to eight times, wrapping downward from the clove hitch. (See figure 16-7[B].) It may be necessary to join another section of rope to the first with an appropriate joining knot. Position this knot on the outside of one of the poles so as not to interfere with the vertical wraps. (See figure 16-7[C].)

- On the last horizontal wrap, continue around the pole that does not contain the clove hitch, pass the rope between the poles below the wraps, and make four to six tight vertical wraps around the horizontal wraps. (See figure 16-7[D].) Make the wraps as tight as possible. The vertical wraps must be as flat as possible next to each other. Insert a carabiner into the last two vertical wraps. (See figure 16-7[E].)

- On the last vertical wrap, pass the rope between the poles above the horizontal wraps. Tie it off with a square knot in the section of rope coming from the clove hitch. Secure with overhand knots tied in the tails. (See figure 16-7[F].)

{{img:0}}

16-29. Use a spreader rope to prevent the A-frame from collapsing from pressure applied at the apex. (See figure 16-8, page 380.) Secure the legs of the A-frame together with a cordelette to fix the maximum spread.

If the ground is soft, dig the legs in about 6 inches. If the ground is a hard surface, anchor the bases of the poles at a 45°-angle to secondary anchor points. The spreader rope should be no more than 6 inches above ground level.

images.caption: Figure 16-7. A-frame horizontal and vertical wraps

sections.heading: Rope Bridges: ANCHORING THE A-FRAME TO THE INSTALLATION ROPE

images.caption: Figure 16-9. Anchoring the A-frame to the installation rope

sections.heading: Rope Bridges: RETRIEVAL
sections.body:
16-32. If the element is crossing the obstacle as part of a longer movement, and there are no follow-on troops, the system must be installed to be retrievable:

- Nearside personnel untie the high-line system maintaining the near side ends of both the installation

rope and belay or tagline rope.

Far-side personnel pull all slack across the obstacle.

- Nearside personnel secure the end of the installation line to the anchor.

Tie a fixed loop in the near side end of the installation rope.

Secure the fixed loop to the installation rope around the nearside anchor with a locked carabiner.

Far-side personnel pull the installation rope tight with several personnel, and then wrap it around an anchor tree with a minimum of two full wraps. Those personnel maintain control of the end of the rope keeping it tight with the tree by hand or can close out the rope by means of two half hitches like the close out on the transport tightening system. Another method is for far-side personnel to build a new tightening system on their side to tighten the rope.

- Nearside personnel attach the tagline to installation line figure eight on a bight using a locked

carabiner and a fixed loop. The tagline remains slack.

- Nearside personnel attach themselves to the installation line in the same way as the main body and

cross the high line.

- Once all personnel are on the far side, the installation rope is unwrapped from the far-side anchor

and allowed to go slack. If a new tightening system was used, it is broken down.

The tagline is then pulled across the obstacle dragging the installation line with it until both ropes are on the far side. Ensure all knots are removed from both ropes before pulling.

sections.heading: Rope Bridges: HIGH LINES
sections.body:
16-33. A high line is a type of suspended rope bridge used to transport equipment or casualties high above difficult terrain that might otherwise be impassable. These can be used for personnel movement as well, although this is less common. The high line is used over large rivers, ravines, chasms, or diagonally from the top of a cliff to the ground below. The system may be established on different planes, varying from horizontal to near vertical. High lines keep the load suspended above the terrain as it travels directly between the near-and far-side anchors.

16-34. High lines come with a high level of risk due to the height of the load above the ground. High lines used for personnel movement require careful calculation to ensure system failure will not occur, resulting in catastrophic fall injury. They should only be constructed by advanced or master military mountaineers who have been formally trained in high-line construction for this purpose.

sections.heading: Rope Bridges: SITE SELECTION
sections.body: 16-35. The crossing site must have appropriate anchors at the near side and the far side and suitable loading and off-loading platforms. If the anchors do not provide enough height to allow clearance, additional height, such as an A-frame, may be used.

sections.heading: Rope Bridges: INSTALLATION
sections.body:
16-36. The same options and tightening techniques used for rope bridges can also be used for high lines; however, due to the higher consequences of rope or equipment failure, a second rope as described earlier must always be used for redundancy. Construction of high lines can be time-consuming and equipment intensive. Installation teams are likely to require additional skills and techniques to get the far end of the installation ropes to the far side of the obstacle.

16-37. Artificial height is used the same way as described for rope bridges.

sections.heading: Rope Bridges: EQUIPMENT RIGGING, BELAYS, AND TAGLINES
sections.body:
16-38. Slings and cordelettes can be used to attach loads to the installation ropes and can be modified as necessary. (See figure 16-10.) Two examples are using two ends of a piece of webbing with a water knot or using a sewn sling. Place a locking carabiner on the high line and place the webbing or sling into it. Bring the bight at the bottom end of the sling up (double it) and clip it into the locking carabiner. A second locking carabiner can now be placed into the two bights. Attach the load by running the long loop of the carrying sling through the load and attaching the bottom loop to the traverse rope carabiner.

{{img:0}}

16-39. Attach a lowering rope to the second locking carabiner in the carrying sling when speed of the load must be controlled. (See figure 16-10.) Standard lowering techniques discussed in chapter 12 can be used.

This rope can be attached to the A-frame using an additional carabiner attached to the carabiner that is in the apex. If Soldiers are crossing, they should hold onto the carrying sling and keep their hands off the installation rope.

16-40. Taglines can also be used as described for rope bridges and are nearly always necessary when the high line does not contain a relatively constant downgrade.

sections.heading: Rope Bridges: RETRIEVAL
sections.body: 16-41. The high line can be retrieved in a manner like the one rope bridge. However, as it is often used to move equipment and casualties, it can be dismantled after it is no longer needed without being retrievable.

sections.heading: Rope Bridges: SECTION II – GUIDING LINES
sections.body:
16-42. A guiding line (see figure 16-11) is an effective means of transporting a litter over uneven, broken terrain (talus) commonly found at the base of cliffs. A guiding line is established and tightened in the same manner as a descending high line using MA but is not tied off once tensioned. The tensioning team retains control of the haul strand and adjusts tension in the installation line as the litter is lowered down it. The litter’s

descent is controlled by a separate team operating the lowering system using a second rope. (See chapter 12 for hauling and lowering systems.) These two teams work together to ensure the litter travels just high enough above the broken terrain to keep movement smooth. Additionally, attendants may move on foot through the terrain to help guide the litter around obstacles.

16-43. The main benefit gained from using a guiding line over a high line is the reduction in risk. Because the guiding line is only tensioned enough to lift the litter in the air, the rope is at a very low risk of being over tensioned and the litter is never high above the ground. Using a high line in the same piece of terrain would usually involve suspending the litter high above the ground on a highly tensioned rope. Additionally, movement down a guiding line is much easier on the casualty than being hand carried through large talus.

16-44. While guiding lines can be a lower risk solution, they can be more complex and are usually more time-consuming. Leaders must ensure that their element is formally trained on guiding lines and has the equipment necessary to accomplish the task safely.
